#9126. ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

Shafeena Yusuff Ali, who has master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact, set up Rizq Art Initiative in 2023 Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”

Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

#9120. Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the ‘turbulence and violence of our times’

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” says Tarini Malik, the curator of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section Sarah Bates

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”

These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”

The Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

#9119. BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million new millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

This matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:

The discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

For FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both new wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% said anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Sources: Chris Hogan National Study of Millionaires, Thomas Stanley "The Millionaire Next Door", Federal Reserve SCF

The path to millionaire status in America overwhelmingly follows a formula, not a lottery ticket:

Millionaires are not "the 1%" — they are the top 10-15%. Here is how wealth is distributed across US households:

Source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022

This means approximately 16% of American households have a net worth of $1 million or more. And the pathway from $500K-$1M (where 11% of households sit) to the millionaire club is often just a matter of continuing to do what they are already doing for another 5-10 years.

The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:

A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

If you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:

The standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as quickly as possible.

The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

The data says this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

Set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

If you are saving 20% or more of your income and investing it in index funds, you are following the exact playbook that created 22 million millionaire households. The only question is timing. At a 30% savings rate, you will get there in approximately 22 years. At 50%, approximately 17 years. The formula is proven, the math is clear, and thousands of FI community members have walked this path before you.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

Overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement plans (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

#9116. The Lumix SHX1 Box-Style Cinema Camera Is The Spirit of Varicam Reborn

The Lumix SHX1 Box-Style Cinema Camera Is The Spirit of Varicam Reborn

Panasonic has announced the Lumix SHX1, the first compact cinema camera to bear the Lumix branding. Previously, Panasonic separated its cinema and consumer imaging divisions between the two brands, but the SHX1 is the unification of the two under one roof.

“For decades, Panasonic has supported the video industry from broadcast to cinema, and its Varicam cinema cameras have been used to make films, dramas and documentaries worldwide. This expertise has also been carried into Lumix, and it led to the Lumix S1H, introduced in 2019 as a cinema-quality professional video model,” Panasonic says.

“In 2024, Panasonic took this further by integrating its professional AV and consumer imaging businesses, which share a commitment to supporting customers’ creativity. The new Lumix SHX1 brings together the expertise of both businesses in a compact cinema camera.”

The combination of the two Panasonic camera divisions and the existence of the SHX1 effectively means the end of the Varicam brand, but should result in a more cohesive overall camera line.

The SHX1 is, effectively, the S1 II packed into a box-style cinema body, with a couple of exceptions. Firstly, Lumix included an anti-aliasing filter to reduce moire at the cost of some sharpness while the camera also offers the ability to shoot BRAW, albeit with a caveat: it can’t capture it to the CFexpress or SD card slot and must instead use an external SSD.

Beyond that, the camera is capable of capturing basically what the S1 II already does. It features a 6K full-frame partially stacked CMOS image sensor with Dual Native ISO and Dynamic Range Boost, giving the camera effectively 15 stops of dynamic range when in V-log. The SHX1 comes with ARRI LogC3 pre-installed as well, allowing users to choose between V-Log and ARRI LogC3.

In standard recording formats, the camera supports 6Kp30 and 5.1Kp60 in 4:2:0 10-bit, as well as in 3.8Kp48 4:2:2 10-bit, which is a new option compared to the S1 II. It also, of course, supports open gate recording and in-camera anamorphic de-squeeze.

The sensor is equipped with a Phase Hybrid autofocus system with 779 points and the SHX1 has the same AI technology as found in the S1 II which enables eye and face detection. Also on-board is Panasonic Lumix's excellent five-axis in-body image stabilization system along with support for Dual IS 2 when combined with a lens that supports OIS and the feature.

Professional interfaces include 12G-SDI and HDMI output, timecode input/output, and internal 32-bit float audio recording through the 3.5mm microphone input. The thermal design supports unlimited recording time in up to 4Kp120 and the design of the box camera means it supports micro V-mount batteries, too. Of note, there is no in-camera ND filter, which is an odd exclusion given the target market.

Panasonic also announced two optional accessories: the XLR Handle Unit AU-XHU1 and the Control Grip AU-GRP1.

The Panasonic Lumix SHX1 is slated to become available in January 2027 for $4,699.99. A kit that includes both the handle and the control grip will be avaialble for $5,499.99.

#9114. Shure’s New MV360 Mics Promise to Make Spatial Audio Capture Easier

Shure’s New MV360 Mics Promise to Make Spatial Audio Capture Easier

Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its new MV360 microphones.

Just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution. Last month, Sony arrived on the scene with its ECM-AX10, a $250 spatial audio mic for content creators. Built with creators in mind, Shure’s new $349 USB-C MV360 is much closer to Sony’s offering in both price and functionality.

Shure says its new MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.

The mono and stereo modes are self-explanatory, working just as they would on a traditional mic. Immersive binaural promises a broader, more lifelike soundstage, which Shure says is ideal for headphone playback. Meanwhile, auto-tracking mode focuses the virtual microphone toward the loudest sound source, such as a speaker in an interview or podcast.

Each Capture Mode records a ready-to-use two-channel file that requires no post-production. However, creators who opt for full 360-degree recording gain significantly more flexibility, as they can edit the Ambisonic B-format (Ambix) file in Shure’s Motiv software or compatible third-party apps.

As Shure explains, the MV360 captures a stronger sense of place than a traditional microphone.

“Listeners can feel closer to a podcast conversation, more immersed in an ASMR scene, or transported into the middle of a bustling market or quiet forest,” Shure says.

The MV360 is a relatively compact spatial microphone housed in an all-metal body. It records and draws power over a single USB-C cable, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of devices, including smartphones and many cameras. Alongside Shure’s Motiv apps, the MV360 supports various third-party applications, allowing users to record 360-degree audio directly to Motiv or a DAW of their choice.

“Sound can make the difference between watching a moment and feeling part of it,” says Eduardo Valdes, Associate Vice President of Global Marketing and Product Management at Shure.

“Until now, capturing that sense of presence has required expensive equipment, technical expertise and time that many creators simply don’t have. The MV360 changes that. It gives creators an easy way to bring listeners closer to the conversation, the performance or the world around them, while giving experienced professionals the control they need to shape every detail,” Valdes continues.

The Shure MV360 is available now for $349 and includes the USB-C mic, a small tripod, cold shoe mic clip, phone clamp, extra cables, carrying case, and windscreen.

Alongside the standard model, Shure also unveiled the MV360+ today, slated to arrive in early 2027. Designed for field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers, the MV360+ works with mirrorless cameras, DSLRs, action cameras, 360-degree cameras, and more. It also adds onboard 32-bit float and internal recording capabilities, a rechargeable battery, and wireless control functionality.

The Shure MV360+ will retail for $449 when it arrives early next year.

#9112. Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

When the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t. Instead, Panasonic is bringing the internals of the S1 II to a new form factor, a cinema box camera, and calling it the SHX1 ($4,699).If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II. PetaPixel Score 7.5/10 ProsClass leading image stabilization never seen in this style of cameraFantastic image quality with minimal rolling shutterExtremely modifiable designConsNo internal BRAW (requires an SSD)Some buttons feel mushy and are difficult to pressNo internal ND filter This is definitely not the FX5 competitor many were waiting for, but it still might make a lot of cinematographers and videographers very happy.

If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

Note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II. If you are unfamiliar with that camera, you can check out our review here. As well, as the SHX1 does not offer any stills capture, this review will be entirely focused on video capture.

The SHX1 is quite compact for a cinema camera, similar to a RED Komodo and weighing only 948 grams (33.4 ounces). In a departure from Panasonic’s previous BG-Series box cameras, this SHX1 includes a top-mounted LCD monitor, with extensive 4-axis articulation and 1.84M dots of resolution.

The articulation is extremely useful, as you can shoot above your eye-line, something usually prohibited with top-mounted displays. There are dedicated exposure buttons on the body, as well as Menu, Back and AF-On. These buttons have a pretty unresponsive feel to them, with little haptic feedback to let you know you’ve actually pushed the button. These can be customized, something I recommend to avoid excessive menu diving.

As expected for a cinema camera, the top, right side and bottom of the camera have plentiful 1/4-inch mounting points for rigs and accessories. The camera is powered by Mini V-Mount batteries, most of which are the same height as the camera. There is an active fan system in the body, which allows even 4K/120p footage to be captured indefinitely.

It’s worth pointing out that you can also purchase the SHX1 with an accessory kit ($5,499), which includes a top handle, XLR adapter and a side grip. The grip feels fantastic but is quite large. I consider it almost a necessary accessory, and the extra controls give operators several more options for custom buttons and a joystick for selecting the autofocus point. The top handle is very sturdy, and the removable XLR adapter gives you easily accessed gain controls. Unlike previous S-Series bodies, which relied on an XLR adapter to capture 32-bit float audio, the SHX1 can record 32-bit audio through the 3.5mm jacks and internal mic as well.

Footage can be stored on a UHS-II SD card, CFexpress Type B card, or external SSD. As expected with a cinema camera, there are locking ports for SDI video, timecode, and a full-size HDMI port. For further external control, a Live Production Unit called the AU-LPU1 will be released in early 2027.

The lack of built-in ND filters is a disappointment, but that was the compromise Panasonic was forced into when keeping the body so small. Screw-in filters or a matte box will be required for controlling light levels.

The sensor is the same full-frame 24.5MP partially stacked unit we saw in the S1 II, which is capable of outstanding results and well-controlled rolling shutter. The only difference is an anti-aliasing filter has been added to minimize incidents of moiré in finely detailed textures.

In my testing, though, I found very similar results to the S1 II, with neither camera giving me moiré even when shooting fabrics at moderate distance.

Like the S1 II, the SHX1 has a massive number of recording resolutions, frame shapes and frame rates. The headline feature is 6K Open Gate recording up to 30P, and 5.1K Open Gate using the full sensor up to 60P. For slow motion, the camera can capture 4K at up to 120P with sound. There is also the option to expand the dynamic range by reducing the readout speed. This does produce appreciably cleaner shadows, but with a corresponding increase in rolling shutter artifacts.

Video can be recorded with MP4, MOV and ProRes codecs for standard 10-bit video. There is also the option to capture 12-bit RAW video in either ProRes RAW or BRAW flavours. Bafflingly, though only ProRes RAW can be recorded to the CFexpress card, BRAW requires an external SSD. This is particularly odd as BRAW offers extremely efficient 12:1 compression rates, which could be easily written to a card. Adding insult to injury, the camera’s startup time is dramatically increased with an SSD attached, taking nearly 10 seconds and often leading to me missing shots.

The video quality itself from the camera is outstanding, with impressive detail and expansive dynamic range even when Dynamic Range Boost is not active. Log video can be captured in either Panasonic V-Log gamma or ARRI’s LogC3. The Panasonic V-Log gamma remains my favourite log curve to work with, but ARRI’s gamma is very flexible and the industry standard in the filmmaking world.

What sets the video quality from the SHX1 apart from any other box camera is the inclusion of incredibly effective in-body image stabilization, based on the S1 II system. This works great in its default mode, but even better when Panasonic lenses are attached and the “Cropless” stabilization is engaged. The camera’s autofocus abilities are also quite reliable, though perhaps not quite as rock-solid as Sony’s and Canon’s more recent implementations. Humans and animals can be automatically detected, and there is a good degree of “stickiness” when following moving subjects.

If you don’t require the box-camera form factor, then the SHX1 can be a confusing proposition. The S1 II features nearly all of the video capabilities with excellent photography specs and an EVF in a considerably more affordable package.

However, many professional videographers and cinematographers require the box-camera design to make it easy to build rigs or mount the camera in a variety of locations. The forthcoming Live Production Unit will add further versatility for using the SHX1 as a remote camera, something the S1 II cannot offer.

As well, if absolute reliability is important, the more robust cooling system in the SHX1 means overheating will not be a concern even when recording demanding footage in hot areas. The S1 II has very good thermals for a hybrid mirrorless camera, but in professional situations absolute reliability is imperative.

Compact cinema cameras like the RED Komodo-X 6K ($4,995) and Blackmagic Pyxis 6K ($2,249) offer similar form factors and outstanding image quality. Unlike the SHX1, these can record extremely compressed RAW video internally. However, the autofocus performance is vastly behind the SHX1, and neither offers IBIS. RED and Blackmagic may offer more bang for the buck for filmmakers, but the SHX1 is the clear choice for handheld documentary work.

RED Komodo-X 6KBuy new on B&HRED Komodo-X 6KBuy used on KEH.comBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy new on B&HBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy used on KEH.com

The Sony FX5 is also a compact full-frame cinema camera with great autofocus and IBIS. The FX5 can accept an optional EVF, has more reliable autofocus and records compressed X-OCN RAW video internally. However, the SHX1 features much more effective stabilization and industry-standard connections. For event work, the Sony makes more sense, whereas the Panasonic will find itself more at home in commercial environments.

Maybe. If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

The Panasonic Lumix SHX1 provides a versatile, box-style platform for filmmakers that integrates high-quality RAW recording, 32-bit float audio, and advanced stabilization. Although it offers a robust feature set for Lumix users, the lack of internal ND filters and reliance on external SSDs for specific recording formats may limit its appeal for some professional workflows.

#9110. Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

Xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China. That also makes them outliers in another respect: they are rare slab smartphones with two displays.

Update 11/17: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated that Pro mode did not support 50-megapixel RAW image capture. It is supported on the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

Both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices. They also feature a rear LTPO AMOLED screen positioned as a creative tool for those who like selfies but want more variety.

Xiaomi already foreshadowed this launch when unveiling the devices at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September 2026, so specs, especially on the camera side, weren’t entirely a mystery. Once they launched in China shortly afterward, the cat was pretty much out of the bag.

We know the main differences between the two phones have to do with screen size, image sensors, the Snapdragon chip, and battery capacity. The 18 Pro Max gets a larger 6.9-inch LTPO AMOLED display (2624 x 1208) with Xiaomi’s own Shield Glass protection, a 1-120Hz variable refresh rate, 4,000 nits of peak brightness, and BT.2020 support. It also runs on the more powerful Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite Extreme chipset and packs a 7,050mAh battery.

Otherwise, the Pro has a smaller 6.4-inch panel (2436 x 1120) with the same display specs as its Max sibling. It also steps down a bit, running on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite chip, and, given its smaller size, has a 6,000mAh battery.

There are slight differences in the rear display size, as the 18 Pro Max features a larger 2.9-inch panel compared to the 2.7-inch screen on the 18 Pro. Both will come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB or 512GB storage configurations, though the Pro Max also offers a 16GB RAM and 1TB storage variant.

Interestingly, Xiaomi equips both phones with almost the exact same camera specs. The three Leica-branded rear cameras are largely identical on both models, with one key exception: the 18 Pro Max uses the LOFIC-equipped Light Fusion 960L sensor, whereas the 18 Pro uses the standard Light Fusion 960.

The 200-megapixel main camera (23mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.28 Light Fusion 960L image sensor and an f/1.67 aperture. Thanks to LOFIC technology, it delivers better dynamic range than both a standard sensor and the 18 Pro’s main camera. You can tell just by pointing both phones at any subject before even snapping the shutter. There’s also optical image stabilization with a CIPA-rated seven stops of shake correction. The Leica Summilux-designed lenses combine precision glass and plastic elements with what appears to be a glare-resistant coating.

The 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera (75mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.56 image sensor, an f/2.4 aperture, and 3.2x optical zoom. Finally, there’s the 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera, whose sensor size remains a mystery. It is somewhat of an outlier in that it’s a 17mm equivalent with a 102° field of view, which is noticeably narrower than most ultra-wide cameras on other phones.

On the software side, Xiaomi adds a new mode called Essential Moment that marries Leica color science with AI-driven image processing to emulate classic film and camera looks. Names like “B&W Film,” “Modern Vintage,” and “Iconic CCD” don’t specify exactly what stock they’re based on, but the new styles add a distinctly Xiaomi-infused element to the camera interface.

This is how Xiaomi frames it: “B&W Film captures the depth and tonal range of classic monochrome photography, Iconic CCD recreates the vivid, saturated colors of CCD-era digital cameras, and Modern Vintage offers refined tones with natural detail for a timeless look. Users can also replicate the optical characteristics of two classic lenses — a 35mm Documentary lens and a 75mm Portrait lens with soft bokeh.”

There are some unusual limitations, however. There is still no 24fps option for video, including in Pro Video. None of the Leica styles and filters introduced in the Leitzphone by Xiaomi have migrated over to these devices, so you retain the same choices offered in other Xiaomi models. Further, while the Pro Max can capture 50-megapixel RAW photos in Pro mode, the standard Pro model cannot.

The Back Display offers a fairly high degree of access to the overall camera interface, including modes, settings, customizations, and more. Xiaomi limits zoom to 0.7x and 1x, meaning there is no way to activate the telephoto camera, though the settings still let you hold up a palm to trigger the shutter hands-free.

While the live preview occupies a sizable portion of the display, Xiaomi configured it to light up in bright white elsewhere to help illuminate subjects in dimmer conditions. It limits available modes to Photo, Video, Portrait, and a retro-style option called Photo Booth, and strangely omits Leica filters from the equation (though you can still choose between Leica Authentic and Vibrant as the overarching style).

You also get the choice to shoot pixel-binned 12.5-megapixel or 50-megapixel stills, with video resolution options ranging from 720p all the way to 8K at either 30 or 60fps. Dolby Vision and a Teleprompter are also available as optional features.

It’s a fully functional display in that it works with swipes and gestures just as the main display does. Tap-to-focus works, as does focus tracking when double-tapping on yourself or another subject in the frame. You can preview shots you’ve taken and either press the onscreen shutter or use the volume buttons to capture a photo or video.

Since the screen uses the rear cameras, the dynamic range advantages apply equally; Xiaomi doesn’t appear to neuter the experience by dialing things back, particularly with the LOFIC sensor on the 18 Pro Max.

An added benefit of the Back Display is that it also works with notifications and real-time information, like calls, maps, ride-hailing, food delivery, audio recording, and more. Pin to Back Display allows you to pin text and images to it for quick reference, such as a boarding pass or QR code. There’s also the option to apply a different wallpaper to it, if you want.

Neither Xiaomi nor Leica made any mention of a photography or teleconverter lens kit for either phone, even as Xiaomi’s Chinese competitors continue to release more of them. There are possibilities there, but you would need a third-party setup to make it work. Thus far, Xiaomi has only made photography kits for its Ultra line, which it maintains is still the company’s flagship with a more specialized photography slant.

You won’t find the Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max in Canada or the U.S. unless you import them yourself. They’re both compatible with North American cellular networks, so there isn’t a hardware limitation in that regard. Warranty challenges aside, Xiaomi is offering five years of Android updates and six years of security updates.

Both models will come in the same four color variants: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue. As for pricing, the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at €1,399, while the 18 Pro Max starts at €1,599.

#9109. Yayoi Kusama sets $15m record as Sotheby’s opens New York mega-sales

Tom Eddison, Sotheby's co-head of contemporary art London, sells Yayoi Kusama's No. 3P.B. Courtesy Sotheby's

Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

Kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a new auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

No. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's

The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's

It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

Not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s said works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, said following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”

On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

Despite Maurizio Cattelan's Comedian selling for a staggering $6.2m, The Now and contemporary auctions in New York made 63% less than last year

The $706m total for the night included a white-glove sale of 24 lots from the collection of late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder

Overall sales were down by around 30% but beyond the disappointing headline figures, women and minority artists shone

Back-to-back auctions, with works from Degas to Banksy, brought in a total of £221m

#9108. The First Known Photograph of Bogotá Sold for Over $331K at Auction

The First Known Photograph of Bogotá Sold for Over $331K at Auction

The earliest known photograph of Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, taken in 1842, has sold for $331,600 at auction.

The daguerreotype, titled Rue de l’Observatoire, was sold by Christie’s this week as part of an auction of 350 photographs from the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion. Roger Therond, was a journalist who served as editor of Paris Match for half a century and spent decades building a collection that brings together major works from the history of French photography.

This image, captured by French diplomat Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros, is not only one of the earliest known photographs of Colombia, but also one of the very first urban daguerreotypes made outside Europe and the United States.

It had been initially listed by Christie’s with an estimated value of up to $89,000, but the photograph far exceeded expectations, selling for nearly four times its estimated value.

The historic daguerreotype shows a nearly deserted street in the Colombian capital with the Andes mountains in the background.

Appointed chargé d’affaires in New Granada (present-day Colombia) in 1838, French diplomat Baron Gros was also a painter and draftsman. Shortly after the daguerreotype was publicly announced in 1839, he began experimenting with the new photographic process in the country. France had made the invention publicly available to encourage its spread around the world. News of the invention was published in the local newspaper El Observador on September 22, 1839. Gros was among the early travelers who recognized the potential of photography as a way to document places, record information, and represent the world around them.

“Photography in those days was, after all, the preserve of an elite; not everyone could afford the equipment,” Élodie Morel-Bazin, the European Head of Photography at Christie’s, tells Reuters. “He was a diplomat; he travelled a great deal; he probably came from a very distinguished family and had the means to devote himself to it. That was his hobby.”

Christie’s says the photograph is particularly remarkable for its 47-second exposure time. Its subject, a view of a city street, was also unusual for the period, when most photographs were portraits. The long exposure meant that people moving through the street were unlikely to appear in the image, leaving the city looking almost empty. The level of detail captured on the metal plate is remarkable, with the Andes mountains visible in the background. The auction house notes that photographing such distant features was technically challenging because haze and diffused light often obscured them.

#9107. Camp Snap’s CS-8 Micro is its Tiniest Camcorder and a Collectible Blind Box Bag Charm

Camp Snap’s CS-8 Micro is its Tiniest Camcorder and a Collectible Blind Box Bag Charm

Camp Snap is tapping into the blind box and bag charm craze with the launch of the CS-8 Micro, the tiniest version yet of its viral CS-8 camcorder, with each camera sold in a blind box that keeps its color a surprise until unboxing.

After launching its CS-8 camcorder last year, Camp Snap introduced the CS-8 Mini — which is less than half the size of the original — earlier this month.

Now, Camp Snap is launching its smallest version of the camcorder yet: the CS-8 Micro. The brand has turned its viral CS-8 camcorder into a fully functional, collectible bag charm that records video and audio. The miniature camera will retail for $39.99.

Each camera comes in a mystery blind box, meaning its color remains unknown until it is unboxed. There are six possible colors to collect: four core shades (Hot Pink, Lilac, Lime and Orange), a rare Classic Black edition and an ultra-rare Glow in the Dark version.

Despite its small size, the 1.5-ounce camera includes several features designed to replicate the experience of using a traditional camcorder. Measuring just 3 inches wide, it records video and audio and is designed to capture everyday moments as short, vintage-style movies.

The camera also features five built-in film-style filters that recreate the appearance of 1990s home videos and classic 8mm film. An LCD screen allows users to frame their shots, but the camera does not offer instant playback. This design encourages users to record footage without immediately reviewing what they have captured.

The CS-8 Micro combines the look of vintage home video cameras with the growing popularity of collectible accessories. Designed to attach to bags, keys, backpacks or zippers, it functions as both a wearable accessory and a working camcorder.

Each CS-8 Micro comes with a pre-installed 4GB microSD memory card, a USB-C cable and a ball chain for attaching the camera to a bag or other accessory.

The CS-8 Micro launches November 16 for $39.99. It will be available through CampSnap.com, as well as at Target and Urban Outfitters, in time for the holiday shopping season.

#9106. Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?

“Yellow River” (1958) was deaccessioned and will be auctioned at Christie's just three years after it was gifted to the museum in 2023.

Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

#9105. VSCO Studio Pro Brings Presets and Streamlined Editing to macOS

VSCO Studio Pro Brings Presets and Streamlined Editing to macOS

When VSCO launched its next-generation editing experience, Studio Pro, on iOS in June, it promised a macOS version later this year. Later is now, and VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is here.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is VSCO’s first-ever standalone photo editor for macOS and promises professional-grade editing features without the complexity or expense of traditional photo editing software.

The app relies on the company’s new Reflex image engine to deliver fast, responsive editing, and it supports RAW files from over 800 cameras made by 20 different brands.

The key focus of the new software is speed, both in image editing itself and across the workflow from capture to delivery. While Studio Pro Desktop does not yet compete directly with industry-standard apps like Lightroom or Capture One in every way, it offers a wide range of image editing tools, batch editing, VSCO’s beloved presets, and integration with existing platform features like Galleries.

The company says it built its new app to enable photographers to move through large sets of images faster and more efficiently without compromising consistency or quality. Again, speed is the focus here.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work,” says Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO.

“75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.”

The new photo editing app is non-destructive, includes over 200 of VSCO’s iconic presets, and offers batch editing for up to 500 images at once. At launch, it supports importing from connected drives, memory cards, and the Photos app. It handles RAW, JPEG, and HEIC files and provides many core image editing tools.

The app includes sliders and tools for exposure, contrast, sharpening, saturation, highlights and shadows, white and black points, clarity, white balance, hue/saturation/luminance, skin tone, vignette, grain, fade, crop, straighten, and more. These hit the key points for many photographers, though more robust tools like masking, curves, and a Remove tool are in development for future updates. VSCO also says that support for projects and culling is in the works.

Once photos are edited, photographers can export their images for social sharing and client delivery, or create and export directly to VSCO Galleries from inside the app.

Alongside VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, the company has unveiled a new, exclusive preset built in collaboration with professional photographer and longtime VSCO user Joe Greer. The new preset, IOE1 Pro, embraces Greer’s distinct style and approach to color.

Greer’s preset delivers warm tones, crisp detail, and subtle saturation. As with all of VSCO’s other presets, users can fine-tune and customize it to match their personal preferences and save their edits as separate, unique presets.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop for macOS is available now for VSCO Pro and VSCO One members. VSCO Pro memberships start at $4.99 per month or $59.99 when billed annually. VSCO One is $41.67 per month or $499.99 annually.

VSCO’s Black Friday deals run through December 4, by the way. With the code “BLACKFRIDAY50,” users can save 50% on Pro and One memberships.

Complete purchasing details and breakdowns of membership tiers are available on VSCO’s website.

#9104. Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

Demonstrators confront police at the Place de la Republique. With more protests expected, Art Basel closed early as a precaution

October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

“It’s important to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024

Of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.)

“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”

Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

#9103. Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.
