The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9101. Photographer Captures Eerie Images of Looming Data Centers in Virginia

Photographer Captures Eerie Images of Looming Data Centers in Virginia

A photographer has set about documenting data centers in northern Virginia — an area that has the highest concentration of data centers in the world.

Stephen Voss’s unnerving photographs show giant box buildings looming over housing developments, baseball fields, and cemeteries.

“Three years ago, I was driving back from a photo shoot in Virginia when I noticed a data center for the first time, in all its drab, boxy glory. Here was the physical reality of something we’ve somehow agreed to call ‘the cloud’,” Voss tells PetaPixel.

The disconnect, Voss says, stuck with him. Over the next three years, he made over 100 trips to data centers in northern Virginia, exploring how these facilities intersect with the communities and places where people live their lives.

“Where does a data center end and someone’s neighborhood begin? What does it look like when the infrastructure behind our digital lives becomes the view from someone’s backyard?” Voss asks.

The project became Every Past and Tomorrow, a book Voss intends to self-publish via Kickstarter.

“Most of us rarely think about the infrastructure behind our online lives — where our photographs are stored, our music is streamed, or an AI prompt gets answered,” Voss says.

“For people living near data centers, those buildings are part of their everyday lives and I don’t think we should discount what it means to live right near one.

“In some neighborhoods, the sounds of cooling fans and natural gas turbines can be heard inside of their homes. People watch their kids play baseball at fields with 75-foot data center walls just past the outfield fence.”

During the course of his project, Voss says he’s witnessed forests cut down, empty fields become enormous buildings, and places where he once made photographs closed off behind fences.

“Every time I return, I see a landscape changing and felt this urgency to document as much of it as possible,” he adds.

Voss says the landscape is changing so much that Google Maps can’t keep up.

“Street View and satellite imagery often show an empty field where there’s already a building,” he says. “So, I spend hours driving around, searching through online permits and county records, and returning to places again and again to see how they’ve changed over time.”

Over the course of the project, Voss gained a drone license so he could take to the air to better show the relationships between data centers and the neighborhood.

However, bringing massive nondescript buildings to life is no easy task, and he started to see the giant blank walls as a canvas.

“I dug through AI research papers, terms of service, and old science fiction,” Voss explains. “At night, I projected words from those texts onto the data centers themselves — returning the language of this technology to the structures that make it possible.”

Voss says that more than once security guards came and spoke to him as he projected text onto the buildings, making him hard to miss.

To support Voss’s book Every Past and Tomorrow: The Physical Landscape of AI, head to his Kickstarter page. More of his work can be found on his Instagram and website.

#9100. Latinx Art’s New Visionaries

Arlene Dávila on the rallying cry of contemporary Latinx artists, Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal, and Martin Puryear’s quiet revolution.

Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. | Arlene Dávila

#9099. A Portrait Photographer Puts 6 Common AI Retouching Myths to the Test

A Portrait Photographer Puts 6 Common AI Retouching Myths to the Test

Photographers have plenty of reasons to distrust automatic retouching. We asked Joe Fraga, a portrait photographer in Salvador, Brazil, to test six of the most common ones on real client work and see which still hold up.

DisclosureThis article is brought to you by Reblum.

Joe Fraga is a portrait photographer based in Salvador, Brazil, who specializes in professional headshots and has worked professionally for nine years (@joefraga on Instagram). Fraga has been a Reblum partner since August 2026. All images in this article are Fraga’s own client work, published with permission.

Few tools divide portrait photographers like AI skin retouching. To some, it is the only way to deliver a fully retouched gallery on time, from a company headshot day to a family session or a wedding. To others, it means plastic faces, data sent who knows where, and software that only knows what lighter skin looks like.

Some of those beliefs come from experience: early beauty filters and automated tools did earn them. But software changes faster than reputations do. So we asked Joe Fraga to take six of the most common objections and test each one against Reblum, a desktop retouching software for macOS and Windows.

The images are Fraga’s, and so are the verdicts. Most of them come from his corporate and headshot work, but the same questions apply to family, fashion, event, and wedding photography.

This is the big one, and it has history. Plenty of retouching software has smoothed faces until the pores vanished, leaving skin that reads as fake from across the room.

Reblum is built on frequency separation, the technique professional retouchers use to avoid exactly that. It splits an image into a layer for color and tone and a layer for fine texture, so blotches can be evened out without touching pores, freckles, and fine hair. In Reblum, the General slider removes blemishes and the Texture slider works on the fine texture itself.

I ran a 24-portrait headshot session through Reblum twice: once on the Natural preset at default settings, and once on Fashion with every slider at maximum. Then I compared both versions at 100 percent.

On Natural, I got the result I need for corporate headshots. The hotspot on the forehead is muted, the redness around the nose and cheeks is calmer, and the pores and the fine lines around the eyes are still there. The beard and eyebrows keep their detail.

Fashion at maximum goes further than most of my clients need. At 100 percent the grain is still there, so it is not the plastic skin this myth describes, but I keep this look for the occasional job that needs a polished finish. For most sessions, I set the sliders at about half and adjust single photos where needed.

This criticism is serious and well earned. Retouching tools trained or tuned mostly on lighter skin have flattened deeper skin tones.

The usual failures are easy to spot: hotspots that turn gray or matte instead of matching the skin around them, and a tone tool that pulls every skin toward one lighter average. Reblum’s Shine Removal blends in color from the skin next to the highlight, and Tone Balance shifts hue, not luminance, so it does not lighten the skin.

I ran four client portraits across a range of skin tones through Reblum (below), plus the portrait at the top of this article.

The fourth portrait is the hardest case in the set: deep, warm skin with strong hotspots on the forehead, nose, and cheekbones. With Shine Removal and Tone Balance, the hotspots came down without turning gray, the skin kept its warm brown, and his freckles are still visible.

Fraga’s Verdict: Busted. On the deepest skin in this set, the hotspots came down and the skin tone did not shift.

This objection has three parts, and all three come from real tools. Many AI services process images on remote servers, so photographers ask where client faces go and whether they train someone’s model. Some charge per image or sell credits, which turns any large job, such as a company headshot day, an event, or a wedding, into a bill. Others make you export everything, edit in a separate app, and import the files again.

Reblum runs on your own computer. Photos are not uploaded, and after a one-time download of the AI model at first launch, it works with no internet connection. The company says client photos are not used to train its algorithms. That also means you can retouch on a plane, in a hotel, or on a studio machine kept off the network.

Batch processing is unlimited, with no credits and no per-photo fees, so one portrait and a full gallery cost the same. Reblum works as a standalone app or as a plugin where you already edit: Lightroom Classic, Capture One, Photoshop.

My workflow is simple. I adjust light and shadows in Lightroom Classic, send the selects to Reblum, and they come back retouched. A typical shoot for me is around 20 photos.

For this test, I took the 24-portrait session from Myth 1 and turned Wi-Fi off. I set the sliders on one image, Reblum applied the same settings to the other 23, and the export took 4 minutes 58 seconds on a MacBook Air M4 at High quality.

Two things to know. Reblum opens DNG files, but it is not a raw processor and does not grade color, so my raw work stays in Lightroom. And batch settings are shared: when one photo needs a different treatment, I switch it to its own settings and adjust it by hand.

Fraga’s Verdict: Busted. The whole session ran offline, with no upload and no credits to count.

A family portrait or a team photo has faces of different ages and skin types, at different angles and distances. Older tools either missed faces or applied the same heavy treatment to everyone in the frame, from a 6-year-old to their grandmother.

Reblum detects every face in the frame. You can retouch them all at once, or pick a single face and work on it alone, for example clearing a teenager’s skin without touching anyone else.

I tested it on a team portrait with three people. Reblum found all three faces; you can see them as Face 1 to Face 3 at the top of the panel. The three have different skin tones and different starting points, so I applied one look to the whole frame first and then went face by face. On the woman on the right, for example, I kept Teeth Whitening low, while another face needed more work on the eyes than on the teeth.

The limit: when you select a single face, Shine Removal and Tone Balance are grayed out, as you can see in the panel. They work on the whole frame only. With three different people in one shot, I would like to set shine for each person. Reblum says separate Shine Removal and Tone Balance settings for each person are planned for an upcoming update. That would solve exactly this problem. For now, I set those two in All mode at a level that works for everyone.

Fraga’s Verdict: Mostly busted. It found and handled all three faces, but Shine Removal and Tone Balance can’t be set per person yet.

Face-only tools leave a mismatch: a smooth, even face above shoulders, arms, and legs that still show redness and blotches. It happens in any shot with visible skin. Boudoir, swimwear, fashion, and wedding work show it most, but so do personal branding and corporate portraits like the one below.

Reblum evens skin on the face and the body. Its skin segmentation finds the skin and separates it from the backdrop, on close-ups and on wide shots. Refine can be set separately for the face and the body, while Shine Removal and Tone Balance work on all skin in the frame together.

I retouched a seated portrait that shows hands and legs. The small marks on the shins and knees are less visible, and the skin on the legs is smoother. The leather skirt keeps its full grain, and the rings and bracelets stay sharp, so only the skin changed.

The hard highlights on the knee and the shin are softer, but the soft light along the legs stays, so the legs keep their shape. With Tone Balance, the red tones on the knees, knuckles, and toes are weaker, and the hands and legs are closer to one color.

What it did not do: the veins on the top of the foot are untouched. If a client wants them softer, that is still manual work.

I would like a separate body control for Shine Removal. The face and the body do not always get the same light: the forehead can have hard glare while the shoulders have only soft highlights. For Tone Balance, one shared control makes sense to me. The tool reads all visible skin together to set the target tone, so face and body match. Separate controls would work against that.

Fraga’s Verdict: Busted. Body skin gets real retouching with its own Refine settings. A separate body control for Shine Removal is the one thing I would add.

There are two fears here. One is a single button you can’t control. The other is software that makes the retoucher, and the retoucher’s craft, unnecessary.

On control: each tool described at the top of this article has its own slider. Tools can be used alone or stacked, and any of them can be switched off to compare. The two presets, Natural and Fashion, are starting points, not final looks.

On replacing the retoucher: Reblum says it handles about 80 percent of the most time-consuming skin work. The remaining 20 percent, a stray hair, a deep crease, very tight close-ups, still needs a person.

Before Reblum, I retouched every portrait by hand, in Lightroom and then Photoshop, at 30 to 40 minutes per photo. Today, in the same amount of time, I finish a whole shoot of around 20 photos.

The creative decisions are still mine, too. I handle the initial edits, including exposure, white balance, rough color grading, and the overall look of the images, before moving on to skin retouching in Reblum.

My manual work afterward is mostly on clothing. Sometimes I also remove a distracting detail from the background, or rebuild part of it with a generative tool in Photoshop. Reblum doesn’t currently have tools for clothing, and Clean Backdrop is made for studio backdrops, not location backgrounds, so that part of the job is still mine.

That gap is already starting to close. A clothing retouching tool is coming later this year, with flyaway hair removal planned after that. Both would help reduce some of the manual finishing work that still falls outside the software.

For now, the biggest change for me is time. The heavy skin work that used to fill most of my editing day is now done by Reblum, leaving me more time to focus on the creative decisions and finishing touches that make each image my own.

Fraga’s Verdict: Partly true. The black box part is busted: every tool is a slider I can see and switch off. The replacement part is half right. Reblum took over the repetitive skin work, not the retoucher. The initial adjustments, color grading, clothing, backgrounds, and final creative decisions are still mine.

Reblum is a retouching tool, not a full editor. Fraga’s tests also turned up a few limits worth knowing before you buy:

Reblum offers a seven-day free trial of the full app, with no photo limit and no credit card. That is enough time to run your own photos past every myth on this list.

After the trial, it costs $11.95 per month billed yearly, $24.90 billed monthly, or $249 for a lifetime license with all updates. Each license covers two computers, and the yearly and lifetime plans come with a 30-day refund. Download it at reblum.app.

Black Friday offer for PetaPixel readers: from November 17 to November 29, 2026, https://reblum.app/p/PetaPixel gives 50% off a lifetime license and 27% off an annual subscription.

Which myth did we miss? Tell us in the comments.

#9098. MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour

Gary Simmons’s High Post (2013) Photo: Jim Prinz, courtesy MCA Chicago

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago

The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”

Government funding for the Sydney institution, which is already closed one day a week and is now charging A$20 entry, remains the same as in 2008

This ups the museums holdings of the artist to 22

The gifted works are predominantly by woman-identifying and Bipoc artists, including pieces by Huma Bhabha, Arthur Jafa, Adrian Piper, Jennie C. Jones and Cindy Sherman

#9097. The TRMNL Frame Is a Gorgeous 31.5-Inch ePaper Picture Frame

The TRMNL Frame Is a Gorgeous 31.5-Inch ePaper Picture Frame

TRMNL, best known for its ePaper screens, is launching a new product that photographers may find particularly appealing. TRMNL Frame is the company’s biggest product to date: a 31.5-inch ePaper display built for showcasing art, including photography, in style.

ePaper picture frames are becoming increasingly common. Just last week, Aura released the Ink 10″, its latest digital picture frame featuring an E Ink screen. Last year, InkPoster arrived in sizes from 13.3 to 31.5 inches, the latter of which matches what TRMNL is doing with Frame.

As TRMNL explains, Frame uses E Ink Spectra 6 technology, powered by TRMNL’s in-house Lazarus color conversion engine. E Ink Spectra 6 has six base colors—black, white, red, yellow, blue, and green—and supports up to three additional custom colors. TRMNL says it will release its dithering algorithms as open-source code, too, so people can tinker with Frame for their own applications.

Since it’s designed to beautifully showcase artwork in the home, Frame needs a frame to match. It comes in a handmade wooden body built by TRMNL itself. The company says it opened a woodshop a few miles from its American headquarters for this new product.

TRMNL says Frame will be available with multiple types of wood, including walnut, white oak, sapele, “and beyond.”

Frame can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation without any additional hardware and also supports tabletop display via a kickstand.

TRMNL says it’s working with developers on several notable features, including an online art platform where people can submit their work and sell it through TRMNL. Frame is network-connected, of course, although users can also display images via a microSD card. The device recharges via USB-C and, since it’s ePaper, will have an extremely long battery life. It will effectively be a wireless digital picture frame.

As Engadget reports, Frame will begin shipping later this year or in early 2027, and the first batch will comprise around 470 units. Frame will cost $1,300.

ePaper displays have come a long way in recent years, and while they still cannot match the color reproduction and sharpness of a traditional LCD panel, they do come significantly closer to replicating the look of a paper print. For photographers, there’s a lot to like about the idea of displaying photos on ePaper, especially as dithering algorithms improve.

#9096. Who Gets Remembered in Art History? New Free Online Course Explores Women Who Shaped Indonesian Art

Co-developed by National Gallery Singapore and independent curator Alia Swastika, the course foregrounds women’s contributions to Indonesian art.

How have women artists shaped Indonesia's cultural, social, and artistic histories? National Gallery Singapore's new free online course, Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower, co-developed with independent curator Alia Swastika, explores this question through the practices and perspectives of leading contemporary artists.

“The absence of women [in historical accounts] does not necessarily indicate a lack of participation.” — Alia Swastika

The course underscores the importance of recovering women’s contributions and bringing overlooked figures and landmark events into view.

Through the work of artists from different generations, regions, and artistic backgrounds, Art and Women in Indonesia highlights a plurality of experiences and perspectives, offering new ways of understanding Indonesia’s histories and their continued resonance in the present.

Structured over five weeks, the course explores the practices of six artists and one collective whose work spans painting, sculpture, installation, performances, and collaborative forms. Together, they illuminate the diverse ways women have contributed to Indonesia’s cultural landscape while engaging questions of memory, power, gender, spirituality, and resistance.

Featured artists include Arahmaiani and Dolorosa Sinaga, whose works confront authoritarianism, censorship, conservatism, and the politics of the female body in public space. Through distinct artistic approaches, they expose the mechanisms through which women’s lives are regulated while fostering critical engagement with urgent social and political issues.

Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower also examines how Nunung WS, Titarubi, and Bakudapan Food Study Group navigate the relationship between individual experience and collective histories. Through installation, abstraction, and collaborative practices, they explore motherhood, cultural memory, care, and everyday labor as ways of engaging with broader social and political structures.

Drawing on Balinese cosmologies and visual traditions, Citra Sasmita and Mangku Muriati foreground female protagonists and goddesses, reworking inherited narratives and transforming painting into a site for feminist interpretation and historical reflection.

Accompanied by exclusive video interviews, readings, and discussion activities, the course provides deeper insight into the artists’ practices and the contexts from which they emerge. It also invites participants to reconsider the role of women in art history and to reflect on how art shapes the histories we remember, the narratives we inherit, and the futures we imagine.

Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower is part of National Gallery Singapore’s series of Online Courses on Southeast Asian Art. Join a growing global community of learners in exploring stories of women, art, and social change in and beyond Indonesia.

#9095. National Geographic Reveals its Pictures of the Year for 2026

National Geographic Reveals its Pictures of the Year for 2026

National Geographic has unveiled its Pictures of the Year 2026, a collection of 25 extraordinary photographs revealing the moments, discoveries, and untold stories that defined the past year.

Selected from more than one million images captured by Nat Geo photographers around the globe, this year’s collection offers a striking look at the natural world, human ingenuity, and the remarkable ways people and wildlife navigate a changing planet.

The images transport audiences from the depths of Greenland’s icy waters to the mountains of Peru, capturing moments of wonder, resilience and discovery that might otherwise go unseen.

Made possible by the unmatched access and expertise of National Geographic photographers, the collection embodies the curiosity, discovery, and spirit of exploration that are distinctly National Geographic.

Among the standout photographs are the first-ever images of moray eels spawning in the wild, captured by photographer Tony Wu after nine months in the field in Japan; a climber suspended from a sea cliff in Spain just after a total solar eclipse; and a spine-tingling encounter with a Greenland shark, one of the planet’s longest-lived vertebrates, photographed by Kiliii Yüyan in the 28.4°F waters of Ammassalik Fjord, among the coldest conditions endured by a Nat Geo photographer this year.

For more on this story, visit Nat Geo Photos.

#9094. The Best Photos From NASA’s Voyager 1 Spacecraft, Which Is Now 1 Light-Day From Earth

The Best Photos From NASA’s Voyager 1 Spacecraft, Which Is Now 1 Light-Day From Earth

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which launched on September 5, 1977, is officially one light-day away from Earth.

Now about 16 billion miles (around 26 billion kilometers) from Earth, Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach this distance. While space enthusiasts are very familiar with the concept of a light-year, a “light-day” is far less commonly used. However, that doesn’t make it any less impressive.

To put Voyager 1’s accomplishment into perspective, if someone flashed a light on Earth right now, it would take an entire day to reach the spacecraft. By comparison, light needs just over 130 milliseconds to circle the globe and about 500 seconds to travel from the Sun—which sits nearly 93 million miles (about 150 million kilometers) away.

Voyager 1 is at a truly mind-boggling distance from Earth. As NASA puts it, “Nothing in the universe travels faster than light. Moving through space about 186,000 miles every second, it crosses enormous distances in a given time period, whether it’s a second, a day, or a year.”

NASA also shared other interesting light-distances. The Moon is 1.3 light-seconds away, even though it took Artemis II astronauts about three days to get there. Neptune, the most distant planet in the Solar System (sorry, Pluto), is about four light-hours and 10 light-minutes away.

Voyager 1 will continue traveling toward AC +79 3888, a star also known as Gliese 445. This obscure star lies more than 17 light-years away, and Voyager 1 is projected to pass within 1.7 light-years of it in a staggering 40,000 years—despite the spacecraft’s cruising speed of nearly 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kilometers per hour).

As for Voyager 1’s sibling spacecraft, Voyager 2, it will reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035. Despite its name and current position behind Voyager 1, Voyager 2 actually launched a couple of weeks earlier. However, Voyager 1 took a faster path through the Solar System. Voyager 2 will never catch up.

It’s unclear just how far Voyager 1 will ultimately travel. Theoretically, it will never stop as long as the universe exists. While interstellar dust could slow the spacecraft or potentially even grind it down to nothing, Voyager 1 would have to hit a lot of dust just to cut its speed in half. Something human beings made, touched with their own hands, and launched into space will travel out into the cosmos forever. Humanity will never truly know what happens to Voyager 1, though, as communications are expected to be lost in about 10 years.

#9093. RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act

The Act survived Republican and Democratic administrations, recessions, and wars, but its health declined precipitously this year after a devastating bout of congressional malpractice. There’s still time to save it.

The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.

Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “the death mask of America.”

NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.

#9092. Worrying Footage Shows Uncontacted Tribe Emerging From Amazon Rainforest to Seek Food

Worrying Footage Shows Uncontacted Tribe Emerging From Amazon Rainforest to Seek Food

An uncontacted tribe in the Amazon rainforest was filmed emerging from isolation to make contact for food in a worrying encounter that highlights the threats to the Indigenous group’s home.

The Awá are Indigenous people living in the Brazilian Amazon. They are among the last remaining hunter-gatherer communities in the region and one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes. With an estimated population of around 350, many of whom remain uncontacted, the Awá face growing threats from illegal logging and encroachment on their ancestral lands.

According to a report by nonprofit advocacy group Survival International, 20 members of the Awá people intentionally approached and made contact with local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon on November 17. The Indigenous tribe asked for yams to take back into the rainforest.

Footage filmed by members of the neighboring Indigenous Guajajara (Tenetehar) people, who support the government station approached by the Awá, shows a group of men, women, and children standing at the forest’s edge. Partly obscured by vegetation, the tribe appears to be naked and wearing necklaces. The men are seen carrying bows and long arrows.

The Awá are skilled hunter-gatherers who traditionally rely on the forest for food and other resources. However, their territory has faced growing pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and cattle ranchers, raising concerns that increasing encroachment may have forced the group to seek help and food outside the forest.

Unexpected contact with outsiders can pose serious risks to isolated Indigenous groups such as the Awá, who have been described as “Earth’s most threatened tribe.” They are particularly vulnerable to diseases against which they have little or no immunity.

Survival International Director Caroline Pearce said the Awá’s decision to leave isolation highlights how forest destruction and encroachment are threatening the survival of Indigenous communities that have traditionally lived independently.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International’s Director Caroline Pearce says in a statement. The uncontacted Awá are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law.”

#9091. North Korea Releases Outrageous Propaganda Photos of Kim Jong Un and Daughter

North Korea Releases Outrageous Propaganda Photos of Kim Jong Un and Daughter

North Korean state media has published a series of propaganda photos starring supreme leader Kim Jong Un and his heir apparent daughter.

The rare images published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) have caused an online sensation thanks to Kim Jong Un’s outrageous pose: smoking a cigarette while sitting on a throne-like chair at a ski resort.

Kim watched as his daughter Ju Ae (although her name has never been officially confirmed) hit the slopes, smiling as she carved the snow.

The photos were taken by KCNA over the weekend, capturing Kim Jong Un and his daughter visiting Samjiyon, a tourist town that’s being built close to the Chinese border. Under construction are Samjiyon airport, a tourist railway line, and a ski resort.

According to KCNA, Kim pronounced the resort’s hotels, lodges​, and housing “flawless and worthy of top marks.”

That his daughter, Ju Ae, features prominently in the photos is telling. South Korean intelligence believes she has been selected as his heir. She is thought to be 13 years old and still in training to take over the Kim dynasty that has ruled North Korea with an iron fist for almost 80 years. She would be the fourth Kim and the first female if she were to succeed her father.

North Korean state media does not publish photos accidentally, and the fact that Ju Ae has been photographed standing shoulder to shoulder with her father carries symbolic weight.

The internet lapped up the North Korean propaganda photos, saying that despotic Kim has “aura.”

#9090. Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

Marble marvels: the Liebieghaus team deduced that the sculpted group on the Parthenon’s east pediment featured the two Dioscuri horsemen seen on this Roman sarcophagus lid at the Galleria Borghese Photo: © Galleria Borghese

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

But now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”

The east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail)

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”

Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”

They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674)

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3

None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027

The Art Newspaper sheds light on the dispute, though the end is not yet in sight

The British Museum has agreed to loan two marble fragments to the Liebieghaus exhibition, which recreates the east pediment of the temple for the first time

The reconstruction of the Acropolis requires the capital and drum back from Britain to be completed, whilst the rightful custody of the marbles is still in question

Acropolis Museum director says the move could pave the way for reunification of works held in London

#9089. Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts

The Ivorian-born painter works only at night, when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest.

Last month, just a couple of weeks before Ouattara Watts’s solo show opened at Karma, I was directed to knock on the cracked glass door of his Bushwick studio. We met in the late afternoon, which is when his studio time begins. The Ivorian-American artist has coffee and a light evening meal, and works all night, before returning home to sleep during the day. To learn why Watts works only at night, one need only look at his paintings. He views art as a portal to the divine; night is when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest, and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest.

Although a gallery representative had told me Watts would be putting “finishing touches” on the paintings for his exhibition at the time of our meeting, I came to realize that he thinks about the work, and his process, without a beginning or end. The centrifugal energy of his rhythmic compositions does not obey edges. Totemic forms continue beyond the bounds of the canvases; arrows point in varying directions; seed pods are split open to reveal concentric circles. His compositions are stained and dripped fields populated by a lexicon of imagery and symbols, developed over the past four decades. They include coffee beans, sacred books, musical notes, serpents, bursting petals encased in atoms, diagrammatic cubes, and mathematical codes.

#9088. Hasselblad X2D II Photographers Can Now Shoot Tethered Into Capture One

Hasselblad X2D II Photographers Can Now Shoot Tethered Into Capture One

Capture One and Hasselblad have jointly announced that real-time, wired tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C is now supported in Capture One with the latest versions of the camera’s firmware and Capture One software.

Tethered shooting support was announced as in the works back in July when Hasselblad first revealed its partnership with Capture One.

“There is a well-documented history between Hasselblad and Phase One, and we’re not here to dwell on it. Capture One has operated as an independent company since 2020, and what matters to us is serving photographers,” Capture One’s CEO Rafael Orta told PetaPixel last summer. “And they have asked us for this for years — on forums, in feature requests, in conversations. That’s why we’ve been working for a while with the Hasselblad team to deliver their shooters a native Capture One workflow.”

Now, not only can Hasselblad photographers edit their X2D II RAW files inside of Capture One, the full studio workflow is supported through tethering. Each image will appear on screen at full resolution at nearly the same moment it is captured when connected with a USB tethering cable. Hasselblad says that photographers can check focus and exposure while the set is still live and nobody has moved.

“[That] means no waiting around or breaking the flow. The full Capture One toolset is available from the first shot, so the grades and masks photographers apply to the first frame carry over to all subsequent shots,” Hasselblad says.

Studio photographers don’t need any convincing as to the value of tethering, but those who are less familiar might not know that the capability is hugely important for commercial sets where clients are on hand. It’s far easier to set clients at a digital tech workstation watching a monitor as results come in rather than hovering over a photographer’s shoulder trying to get a look at the rear LCD.

“This means creative direction and collaboration happen in real time, turning every session into a truly collaborative shoot,” the two companies add.

“We are always listening to our photographers, and tethering support for Hasselblad cameras was one of the top requests when our collaboration with Capture One was announced earlier this year,” Bronius Rudnickas, Global Marketing Manager at Hasselblad, says. “We are delighted that this workflow option is now available, giving Hasselblad photographers and creatives worldwide greater flexibility in their creative journeys.”

Wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C is available starting today in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Mobile 4.3.0, requiring X2D II 100C firmware version 1.4.15.7.

#9087. LeBron James Sues Sports-Betting App for Using AI-Generated Images of Him

LeBron James Sues Sports-Betting App for Using AI-Generated Images of Him

NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app for allegedly using AI-generated images of him in its marketing.

On Tuesday, James filed a lawsuit in the Southern District of New York against the founders of Bron, an AI-powered sports-betting app. The lawsuit focuses on a video ad released by the Bron app’s founders earlier this month. It shows an AI-generated version of James using the Bron app to bet on basketball games from a locker room.

According to the complaint, the ad depicts James wearing a basketball jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23. It also reproduces his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video shows the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app.

“The ad catapulted the Bron app from obscurity to controversy, with the ad gaining a million views within a day — exactly as defendants intended,” James argues in the civil complaint, according to a report by Courthouse News Service.

The complaint also says the AI-generated image of the basketball star “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player ​performance—conduct that NBA rules prohibit.”

James argues that the depiction of him sitting in a locker room and betting on basketball could also harm his reputation.

“This is at odds with Mr. James’s well-known and highly televised routine of being on time for games and being one of the first people out on the court,” he argues.

James also claims that the app’s name was chosen to attract attention by exploiting his well-known “Bron” nickname. He accuses PlayVision, the company that operates the app, and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, of deliberately using the name to mislead consumers into thinking he endorsed or was affiliated with the product.

James’s lawyers sent the company a cease-and-desist letter on November 5. Following the letter, the startup removed the ad from X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) and Instagram and said it was working to change the app’s name, according to the complaint. However, the lawsuit alleges that the video remained available through third-party reposts and that the company had not changed the app’s name by the time the lawsuit was filed.

LeBron’s lawsuit comes after Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland sued an airline last month over a social media post that featured an edited image referencing his distinctive hairstyle during the 2026 World Cup.

#9085. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

#9084. Photographer Encounters Legendary Grizzly Bear Known as ‘The Boss’ Ahead of Hibernation

Photographer Encounters Legendary Grizzly Bear Known as ‘The Boss’ Ahead of Hibernation

A photographer had an incredible encounter with a famous grizzly bear known as “The Boss” in Banff, Canada.

Jason Leo Bantle was in Banff National Park when he came across fresh bear tracks in the snow. Knowing the big bruin must be in the area, Bantle came back on November 6 and spotted The Boss foraging along the railway tracks that run through the park.

“Known for grains being dropped from railcars or other animals being hit, The Boss has learned that when food is not plentiful in the backcountry, the tracks may offer some subsistence,” Bantle tells PetaPixel.

Bantle is aware of the risks of approaching a grizzly in the wild, so he waited at a great distance, observing the bear through an 840mm telephoto lens and binoculars.

The New York Times ran an article over the weekend about The Boss. It revealed that he is categorized as “habituated” by the park’s management, which means he is not bothered by people so long as he is left alone.

“The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Paul Klra, a gas station owner and photographer, told The Times. “He has never done any harm to anyone.”

While The Boss has never done any harm to humans, he certainly has done harm to other bears. His biggest rival in the area is a bear called Split Lip; The Boss gave him that lip.

He’s also survived being struck by a train and has been known to kill and eat black bears. However, a park ecologist tells The Times that 90% of The Boss’s diet is made up of berries, roots, and other plants.

“As a professional photographer, you are focused on your craft and capturing an image that is the essence of the animal and their environment, so you do lose yourself in the moment,” Bantle says of photographing The Boss.

“I always reflect back on moments like this with The Boss; he is a living legend! The one image of him as he lumbered toward me with light snow falling was just magnificent: the grandeur of this bear, an apex predator, yet the gentleness of his quiet presence — no wind and a light snowfall, it was humbling to be in his presence.”

The Boss is thought to be 28 years old, advanced for a bear. He has become internationally famous, and it makes the news when he comes out of hibernation.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.
