#9056. Sotheby’s makes last-minute deal to sell $180m Van Gogh painting following dispute

The Blaquier family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) in 1975

Sotheby’s today announced that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in New York.

The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”

The provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”

The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

Looted by the Nazis, after the war it was returned to the Rothschild family

#9054. Mexico's Parque del Jaguar protects jaguars with 18-kilometre limestone wall

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

Rather than creating a conventional enclosed nature reserve, Colectivo C733 designed a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals‘ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The park occupies a coastal territory containing tropical forest, mangroves, underground rivers and karstic geology, as well as the ancient Mayan archaeological site of Tulum.

Its landscape had also been affected by contaminated soil around a former airstrip and habitat disruption caused by the Cancún-Tulum highway.

At its perimeter, the studio added an 18-kilometre dry-stacked limestone wall, known locally as a tecorral, informed by traditional Mayan stone boundaries.

Built without mortar, the wall allows wildlife to move through gaps between the stones while establishing a physical boundary around the protected area.

Within the park, Colectivo C733 introduced a number of public buildings and viewing platforms, concentrating new construction in previously altered areas and leaving large sections of the territory untouched.

Low-impact transport routes, including pedestrian and cycling paths, connect the different areas, with electric transport also introduced to reduce the impact of visitor movement.

The routes link the park’s public facilities with its archaeological and ecological sites.

At the central entrance, a timber-framed building is screened by closely spaced vertical wooden members and topped with a woven palm-thatch roof.

The complex accommodates a museum, cafe, shop, multipurpose room and open-air forum, alongside a kitchen designed for cooking over smoke.

Other structures include elevated observation towers and a long suspended walkway that crosses the forest canopy, revealing different aspects of the area’s geology, water systems and biodiversity as visitors move through it.

“By designing how the territory is revealed, inhabited, and understood over time, Parque del Jaguar shifts architecture from a static intervention to an evolving framework that connects environment, culture, and collective awareness,” Colectivo C733 said.

Access is more controlled in sensitive areas, helping to limit disturbance to wildlife habitats, including those used by jaguars.

At the coast, stone platforms, stepped seating and raised timber staircases provide access to viewpoints overlooking the Caribbean Sea.

The buildings use locally sourced limestone, chicozapote timber, sascab – a naturally occurring limestone-based material – and palm thatch.

Green roofs, shaded outdoor spaces and naturally ventilated structures help reduce the need for mechanical cooling in the tropical climate.

Alongside the construction work, the project includes soil remediation, reforestation and the recovery of natural water systems.

Asphalt has been removed from previously developed areas as part of efforts to restore the ground and reconnect habitats.

Founded in 2019, Colectivo C733 brings together the practices of Gabriela Carrillo, Carlos Facio, José Amozurrutia, Eric Valdez and Israel Espín to work on public architecture and urban infrastructure across Mexico.

Its other projects featured on Dezeen include a square-shaped pedestrian pier that hovers over a lagoon in Bacalar, Mexico and a brick music school topped with a cantilevered coconut wood roof in Nacajuca, Mexico.

#9052. Taylor Swift’s Costumes and Instruments Are Coming to the MFA Boston

Taylor Swift’s sellout tour “The Eras Tour” traveled to 21 countries and 51 cities between 2023 and 2024 with many outfit changes and props on tour that became viral. A selection of those rhinestone-covered costumes, among other archive pieces, will be the subject of an exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, titled “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection,” scheduled to run from April 10, 2027 through August 15, 2027.

Fans can expect to see instruments and objects representing the 12 eras of her musical career, starting “Tim McGraw,” a single on Swift’s self-titled debut album in 2006, including a custom red Alberta Ferretti gown worn during the “Folklore” and “Evermore” sets in 2020; a bejeweled Zuhair Murad bodysuit that she wore in 2022; and more from her latest album, 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl”. Related Articles Taylor Swift Fans Flock to Friedrich Heyser's 'Ophelia' at the Wiesbaden State Museum in Germany Swifties Visit Wiesbaden State Museum to See Friedrich Heyser's 'Ophelia', 'Black Artists Matter' Street Mural Faces Removal in Austin, and More: Morning Links for October 15, 2025

“This is the first exhibition in the MFA’s history devoted to a musician, and we’re thrilled to invite visitors for an up-close look at the fashion and instruments of one of the most influential cultural figures of our time,” Kristen Hoskins, the museum’s director of public programs, said in a statement. “I’m excited to welcome audiences across generations to this unique experience at the museum—especially Swifties, whose passion and community building are an essential part of Taylor’s story.”

Beyond dresses, the exhibition will provide deeper look at her practice. The show will include several instruments, such as a Deering banjo from the “Speak Now World Tour” in 2010, a green Gibson J-180 acoustic guitar from the “Reputation Stadium Tour” in 2017 and a mandolin from the music video for “Willow” in 2020. The museum said its goal is to take Swifties, and non-Swifties, on a journey through the super star’s career, which currently boasts more than 245 million album sells worldwide.

“With over a century of experience celebrating the art of musical instruments and fashion, the MFA is the perfect place to host an exhibition exploring Taylor Swift’s exceptional artistry,” Jared Katz, the museum’s curator of musical instruments, said in a statement.

The MFA is not the first museum to dedicate gallery space to Swift. In 2024, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London showcased 16 looks worn by the pop star during her “The Eras Tour,” which was attended by Tom Cruise to Prince William, and his children, Princess Charlotte and Prince George.

#9050. The Most Expensive Works by Wassily Kandinsky Ever Sold

Few modern artists have proven as reliably sought after as Wassily Kandinsky, the Russian modernist rightfully deemed the father of abstract art, and few have rewritten their own auction record as often. The ascent charted here is steady rather than meteoric: records have tended to fall by razor-thin margins, sometimes by less than a million dollars, and in one case, at Sotheby’s London in 2017, the mark was broken twice in under an hour. Each new high nudged the ceiling higher, rather than shattering it outright.

That changed on Tuesday. At Christie’s New York’s 20th century evening sale, the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922-23) sent Kandinsky record soaring to $85.8 million, good for nearly double his previous auction high.

In Kandinsky’s view, painters were akin to prophets, and logically, the apocalypse would follow: a cataclysmic collapse of tangible reality, spiritual rapture, and figuration giving way to abstraction. Zum Thema Jüngstes Gericht (On the Theme of the Last Judgment), with its deluge of yellow unleashed upon the canvas, captured the religious fascinations that fueled his creative inquiries. The work is “bristling with the exciting energy of avant-garde abstraction,” our reporter wrote in November 2018, when it appeared at Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern art evening sale (the same sale at which Improvisation on Mahogany set the record benchmark). It sold to an anonymous telephone bidder for $22.8 million, against an estimate of $22 million to $35 million.

Kandinsky’s Study for Improvisation 8 (1909), a cardboard and canvas work, was the highlight of Christie’s November 2012 Impressionist and Modern art auction in New York. The auction house expected it to fetch $20–$30 million, matching the $20.9 million record Sotheby’s obtained for Fugue (1914) in 1990. It was a safe bet: the work sold for $22.8 million.

Fully realized Improvisation studies rarely appear at auction; most of the finished pieces landed in museum collections. The final numbered work in the series, Improvisation 8 is a semi-abstraction set in a hilltop fortress. In it, a man wields a sword in Old Kiev, the medieval district of modern-day Ukraine, amid kneeling pilgrims—mystical spirituality-lite, relative to his later works. The piece was exhibited at Tate Modern, Kunstmuseum Basel, and Fondation Beyeler, but before it came to auction, it had mostly been on loan to the Kunstmuseum Winterthur in Switzerland, where it had hung since 1960.

It’s forgivable to forget the auction record set by Tiefes Braun, one masterwork among many to appear in “Visionary: the Paul G. Allen Collection”, the largest single-owner art auction in history. The sale generated more than $1.6 billion over its two-day run at Christie’s in November 2022 (The opening night alone brought in $1.5 billion.) For a refresher: Tiefes Braun went to an unnamed buyer for $23.2 million. That, along with its history, makes it a significant work, at least by Kandinsky standards.

Kandinsky joined the faculty of the Bauhaus in 1922, finding it fertile ground for his experiments in expressive abstraction. Out of them grew Tiefes Braun, a psychological portrait of shape, color and space. According to Christie’s, Tiefes Braun was exhibited widely by Kandinsky through the mid-1920s, and formerly in the collection of the Guggenheim, which acquired it from the estate of the art dealer Karl Nierendorf. Allen, the late Microsoft co-founder, purchased it from the museum in 2000.

It was no shock that Rigide et courbé broke the artist’s record when it appeared at Christie’s New York Impressionist and Modern sale in November 2016. The 1935 work was estimated to fetch between $18 million and $25 million, placing its $23.3 million finish squarely within expectation. The painting was acquired in 1936 by Solomon Guggenheim directly from Kandinsky and was last exhibited by a museum in 1949. It had been held by the same family since acquiring it at Sotheby’s in London in 1964.

Measuring at 45 by 63.5 inches, the painting “ranks alongside the biggest pictures of his last years,” Conor Jordan, the deputy chairman of Impressionist and Modern Art at Christie’s, said in 2016. Christie’s also said the picture marked Kandinsky’s first experiments with sand. “He may have been inspired by Georges Braque, who often used sand, particularly in paintings from the 1920s and 1930s,” Jordan added.

Improvisation auf Mahagoni (Improvisation on Mahogany) was completed while Kandinsky was putting the finishing touches on his treatise, On the Spiritual in Art, and the two make a perfect pairing. The treatise envisioned non-objective art as the soul’s portrait, compelled onto canvas by spiritual imperative. Improvisation auf Mahagoni is theory in practice: a tapestry of jewel tones applied in staccato brushstrokes, caught mid-pulse like a frozen metronome.

It arrived at Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern art evening sale in November 2018 alongside two other Kandinskys, Le Rond Rouge (1939) and Zum Thema Jüngstes Gericht (1913). Selling for $24.2 million against an estimate of $15 million to $20 million, it proved the most coveted of the three, falling a few million dollars short of the night’s top lots, a Magritte and a Schiele. The painting did, at least, spark “a round of appreciative applause in the York Avenue salesroom,” according to our reporter.

Given the significance of Kandinsky’s “Murnau” works within his artistic evolution, their appearance at auction is a notable event. When Murnau – Landschaft mit grünem Haus (1909) came up for auction at Sotheby’s London in June 2017, the auction house praised it as an elusive “masterpiece,” the work having remained in the same Swiss family collection since the 1920s. It arrived with an estimate of £15 million to £25 million and sold for £20.9 million ($26.5 million), surpassing the artist’s previous auction record of £13.5 million ($21 million) set in 2013.

But as noted below, top lot is a tenuous honor when the competition is the artist himself, and the same sale saw another record broken when Kandinsky’s 1913 Painting with White Lines came to the block six lots later. Both Kandinsky paintings helped push Sotheby’s evening total to £149 million ($187.7 million), a 45% jump from the previous year’s comparable sale, giving the London blue-chip art market a much-needed boost of optimism.

The two top lots on this list speak to the value of Kandinsky’s early 20th-century steps toward abstraction. Tensions calmées, painted decades later, presents a world of biomorphic forms that is far more fantastic. As Sotheby’s noted when offering the painting at its London sale in June, 2021, the work’s formal language is full of contradictions, as its title suggests. “The structural logic of the Bauhaus meets Surrealist fancies that, rather than fight, flow along his soundscape,“ the auction house wrote.

Painted in Paris in 1937, Tensions calmées was one of 50 Kandinsky works famously sold off by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation in London in 1964—the first in the world devoted entirely to a single modern painter, according to Sotheby’s. (The New York art world, meanwhile, was outraged; a foundational patron of the Guggenheim described it as “a tragedy for the United States,” to the New York Times.)

Willard Gidwitz, of the Helene Curtis family, scooped up the piece, and it spent 57 years in the family’s private collection before his heirs consigned it to Sotheby’s. After brisk bidding, it left the block at £21.2 million (roughly $29.3 million), within its presale estimate range of $24.8 million to $34.4 million, but just enough to break a record.

On October 14, 2026, Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben arrived on the block, heralded by Christie’s London auctioneer Adrien Meyer as “the most important early work by the artist to ever come to auction.” The panoramic procession of peasants, pilgrims, and folkloric beings teeters between figuration and abstraction. The characters are recognizably human but not of this world, rendered in an acidic palette that reads like a psychedelic trip.

According to our reporting, bidding opened in a flurry, with around 20 competing claims in the opening salvo alone. The most determined bidders were Christie’s specialists Amelia Walker, Katharine Arnold, and Maria Los, with Los ultimately securing the painting on a £27 million ($35.7 million) hammer bid, clearing its high estimate of £25 million before fees. With fees, the final price came to £31.56 million ($41.5 million).

Originally acquired by the Dutch collector Emanuel Lewenstein in 1907, the painting disappeared during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands in 1940. It reappeared on long-term loan at Munich’s Lenbachhaus from the Bayerische Landesbank. In 2023, it was restituted to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann, amid a push from the German government to reunite Nazi-looted art with its rightful owners and following decades of legal action.

Sotheby’s June 2017 Impressionist and Modern art sale in London was one to remember thanks entirely to Kandinsky: the artist’s record was broken twice in less than an hour. First, Kandinsky’s Fauvist-era landscape of Murnau from 1909 went to a phone bidder for £21 million ($26 million). Its reign was short-lived. Six lots later, Painting with White Lines came to the block with a guarantee in excess of $35 million (£27 million) from, if rumors are to be believed, mega-collector Ronald Lauder. A rarely available example of Kandinsky’s foray into abstraction, the picture had left Russia for the first time in 1974, when the Cologne collector William Hack acquired it from the State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow. His heirs brought it to Sotheby’s.

Four bidders battled for the work, which was ultimately won by an Asian phone bidder for £33 million ($41.6 million) “to thunderous applause—especially from Sotheby’s staff,” according to Artnet News.

Kandinsky’s Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) (1910) depicts the Bavarian village of Murnau, nestled in the foothills of the Alps, in vibrant brushstrokes that experts say heralded Kandinsky’s turn toward abstract art. At Sotheby’s London in March 2023, it set the artist’s auction current auction record of $44.7 million.

Ahead of the painting’s sale, Helena Newman, chair of Sotheby’s Europe, said that “Kandinsky’s Murnau period came to define abstract art for future generations, and the appearance of such an important painting—one of the last of this period and scale remaining in private hands—is a major moment for the market and for collectors.” Lucian Simmons, Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of restitution, added that the timing of the sale carried particular weight: 2023 marked the 25th anniversary of the conference that established the architecture for the restitution of artworks looted by the Nazis.

According to Sotheby’s, the painting hung in the dining room of Johanna Margarete Stern-Lippmann and Siegbert Stern, founders of a textile company and collectors whose vast collection included works by Renoir and Munch, among other masters. After the Nazis rose to power, Stern died, Stern-Lippmann died in Auschwitz, and the collection was looted. In the early 2010s, the painting was discovered at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, Netherlands, where it had been since 1951. A long legal battle ensued, before it was restituted to the 13 descendants of the Stern family in 2022.

“Though nothing can undo the wrongs of the past, nor the impact on our family and those who were in hiding—one of whom is still alive—the restitution of this painting that meant so much to our great-grandparents is immensely significant to us, because it is an acknowledgement and partially closes a wound that has remained open over the generations,” the family said.

Betonte Ecken (1922–23) measures just over four feet square and is marked by dynamic, abstract geometric shapes; the four corners are each pointed to with strong shapes and lines, in keeping with its title, which translates as Accentuated Corners.

The painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, then going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay. She was then the principal adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to New York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the Nahmads.

On November 17, the painting changed hands again, when it sold at Christie’s 20th-century evening art sale. It hammered for $74 million; with the house’s fees, the final sale amount was $85.8 million. The work sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, Sara Friedlander, chairman of post-war & contemporary art, Americas at Christie’s, and art advisor Ralph De Luca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid. —Brian Boucher

#9049. Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, Cambridge, Massachusetts Photo: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”

Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Records show how masters retained power over enslaved people even after emancipation

Archaeologists have uncovered more than one million objects on the site

The repatriation, from a private collection in Detroit, is the largest of its kind in Brazil’s history

#9048. Japanese sauna by Daichi Inc makes "people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest"

Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

“Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials,” said the studio.

“In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment,” it added.

“Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself.”

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna’s structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site’s natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

“Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework,” said the studio.

“Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest,” it added. “The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

#9046. A Wassily Kandinsky Sold by the Nahmads Fetches $85.8 M. at Christie’s, Notching a New Auction High

At Christie’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday night, a painting by Russian-born pioneer of abstraction Wassily Kandinsky notched a new high at auction when it hammered for $74 million; with the house’s fees, the final sale amount was $85.8 million.

Betonte Ecken (1922–23) carried a $60–$80 million estimate and was guaranteed to sell by the house, financed in full or in part by a third party, as noted in the sale catalogue. Christie’s confirmed to ARTnews ahead of the sale that it was bound to sell at a record-setting level. It was tied for the highest-estimated lot in the house’s marquee November sales with a landscape by Austrian market titan Gustav Klimt, also on Tuesday. Related Articles Rare Artist-Designed Louis Vuitton Handbags Included in Upcoming Christie's Upcoming Online Sale Amid Legal Controversy, Christie's Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction

The work sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, Sara Friedlander, chairman of post-war & contemporary art, Americas at Christie’s, and art advisor Ralph De Luca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid.

The seller was the prominent Lebanese-American Nahmad family, which acquired the canvas at Sotheby’s New York in 1986, ARTnews revealed in October; according to Sotheby’s, it hammered at that sale for $1 million. (It had also come to market at the same house in 1964, when it hammered for $61,000.) The art-dealing dynasty’s holdings are reputed to include as many as 5,000 artworks, collectively worth upwards of $4 billion.

Kandinsky’s previous high was $44.8 million, paid for the artist’s 1910 painting Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) at Sotheby’s London in 2023. Some 14 Kandinsky canvases have fetched prices north of $20 million since 1990, according to the Artnet auction price database; all but one has sold since 2012. His third-highest price, $41.8 million, was achieved in October, when Christie’s London sold his 1907 painting Das Bunte Leben (La vie mélangée).

Betonte Ecken measures just over four feet square and is marked by dynamic, abstract geometric shapes; the four corners are each pointed to with strong shapes and lines, in keeping with its title, which translates as Accentuated Corners.

The painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, then going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay. She was then the principal adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to New York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the Nahmads.

Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky published the book On the Spiritual in Art in 1911 and was part of the influential Blaue Reiter group. After his first solo exhibition, at Der Sturm gallery in Berlin in 1912, one of his works was included in the groundbreaking 1913 Armory Show exhibition in New York. He lived in Russia from 1914 to 1921, mainly in Moscow, where he maintained a position at the People’s Commissariat of Education, until moving to Weimar in 1922. His first New York solo was in 1923, organized by Société Anonyme, the organization founded in 1920 by Marcel Duchamp, Katherine Dreier, and Man Ray.

Kandinsky became a German citizen in 1928, but would relocate to France when the Nazi government closed the Bauhaus in 1933, becoming a French citizen in 1939. The Nazis seized dozens of his works in the party’s campaign against “degenerate art.” Kandinsky died in France in December 1944, three days short of his 78th birthday and six months shy of Germany’s surrender to Allied forces.

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

As rumours about the casting of the next James Bond began to hot up this week, my phone has been busy. Most of my friends (hello, both!) know me as a huge James Bond fan, and have wanted to know who I thought was going to get the role. Well, one thing's for sure, I told them all. It won't be Pattinson. Mark my words. He's just too famous.

So you can imagine my surprise when Robert Pattinson was indeed announced as the new James Bond this afternoon. Everything about the news feels bizarre to me, including the lack of press release and associated fanfare (whereas Daniel Craig rode down the Thames on a speedboat, Pattinson was announced via a simple social media post). But the biggest shock is that Pattinson is by far the most famous person to be cast in the role. He's the first bonafide A-lister to pick up the Walther PPK. He's Batman, for God's sake. For better or worse, the Bond brand changed forever today. And it's thanks to one name: Amazon.

It perhaps isn't surprising that Blofeld's—sorry, Bezos's—company has opted for such a bankable star. The company paid billions to acquire MGM (which owned the rights to Bond), and will want a return on its investment. But the whole thing seems so at odds with the ethos of the previous Bond custodians. "I felt I had to have an unknown actor, not a star," producer Cubby Broccoli said of the search for the very first Bond. "Above all, a man you’d believe could be James Bond."

For decades, Bond has been one of the most carefully controlled brands in entertainment. The gun barrel sequence, the theme tune, the 007 logo, the Aston Martin; every element is instantly recognisable, and has been meticulously protected by the Broccoli family. Bond films have always felt like events, partly because they don't come along very often. But Amazon doesn't do scarcity, it does content. And with the company now in creative control of the franchise, it's hard not to wonder how long it will be before 007 becomes less of a cinematic institution and more of an endlessly expandable IP. I'm not sure I'm ready for the 'Young Q' spin-off.

There are, of course, opportunities here. Bond has arguably been in need of a shake-up for some time, and Pattinson is a genuinely exciting actor, capable of bringing something strange, unpredictable and perhaps even uncomfortable to a character that has occasionally felt trapped by his own iconography. But the choice also feels like a statement of intent from Amazon. Where previous Bond actors were largely blank canvases onto which the 007 identity could be projected, Pattinson arrives with a huge, established brand of his own. Rather than making a star out of Bond, Amazon has bought a star to sell Bond. It's a subtle distinction, but a significant one. Am I going to be able to look up at the screen and see James Bond, rather than Robert Pattinson in a suit?

But while it'll be Pattinson's name that hogs the headlines, the bigger question isn't simply what kind of Bond Pattinson will be, but what kind of brand Amazon wants Bond to become. Will the company recognise that Bond's enduring appeal lies partly in his exclusivity, his mystique, and his ability to remain just a little out of reach? For all of his reinventions, 007 has always felt bigger than the actor playing him. Until today.

#9043. Modigliani sculpture heads Phillips’s New York evening sale at $44.6m

Modigliani’s Tête led Phillips's auction last night, selling for $44.6m

A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”

Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

On the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

The piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s New York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

Rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

The night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982)

And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

Nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

Led by a once-scandalous Modigliani painting, the £296.3m London evening sale provided a bright spot for a market struggling with concerns of Brexit and overseas competition

The auction house’s bottom line benefitted from the strong performance of works from the collections of S.I. Newhouse and Paul G. Allen

#9042. The Most Expensive Works by Gustav Klimt Sold at Auction

In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. On Tuesday, Christie’s added another landmark sale to the list, when it sold the 1915-1916 landscape Litzlbergkeller for $82.3 million.

Klimt’s highest results now count among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 11 paintings discussed below.

Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity.

Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement.

First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

From 1900 until his death in 1918, Klimt often spent his summers in the Austrian countryside on the shores of Lake Attersee,. It was during his summers there, in Litzlberg, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. The 1915-1916 canvas Litzlbergkeller presents a view focused on the Litzlberg Cellar, a brewery and inn on the north shore where Klimt stayed during his first several summers in the area, but actually dates from a decade after his move to a cottage on the lake’s southern shore. The artist partly based the composition on his own study via a telescope from the opposite shore and partly on postcard views.

The piece was commissioned by banker and entrepreneur Otto Primavesi, who, with his wife Eugenia, was a major patron of the arts and commissioned Klimt to paint two family portraits in 1912. It went by 1927 to Austrian photographer and anthropologist Hugo Bernatzik; then to Vienna collector Kurt Wieser, who owned it from the ‘30s until at least 1958; and from there to Serge Sabarasky, a cofounder of New York’s Neue Galerie and a major promoter of Klimt’s work. In its long life, it has hung on the walls of museums and institutions such as Secession Vienna; the Künstlerhaus in Vienna; the Musées Royaux des Beaux-Arts in Brussels; Palazzo Strozzi in Venice; Kunsthaus Zürich; and the Leopold Museum in Vienna.

In May 1997, Sotheby’s New York sold the work from the estate of Sabarsky, who died in 1996, for $14.7 million. Adjusted for inflation, that’s about $30.9 million On November 17, the work returned to the auction block at Christie’s, where global president Alex Rotter, and Max Carter, the house’s global chairman, battled for the work in an extended five-minute back-and-forth. The work hammered at $71 million, with Rotter taking the winning bid. With the house’s fees, it fetched $82.3 million. —Brian Boucher

Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière, who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case.

On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

“I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald), he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface.

Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914.

Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush.

First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918.

The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer.

At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a new auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest, highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography.

Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation.

Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi.

#9041. Arudeko transforms discarded wool into paper-like material

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

“Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

“Bianni was born from the idea of giving new life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” said Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

“No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she said. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”

Throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

#9039. Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons’s Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie’s, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso

Collectors and the public are getting another look at that collection this week. Nine works consigned to Christie’s New York came from the artist’s holdings, according to two unnamed industry sources who spoke to the Times this fall. The sources said the house had guaranteed Koons a minimum price and that he planned to plow the proceeds toward his famously expensive art production. (Christie’s has identified the seller only as “a distinguished collector.”) Related Articles A Wassily Kandinsky Sold by the Nahmads Fetches $85.8 M. at Christie's, Notching a New Auction High Rare Artist-Designed Louis Vuitton Handbags Included in Upcoming Christie's Upcoming Online Sale

Seven of the works, grouped under the title “Heroes and Lovers,” were offered at the house’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday. Together they were estimated at $104 million to $153.5 million. The low end alone is slightly more than the $91.1 million Christie’s got in 2019 for Koons’s own 1986 sculpture Rabbit. The other two works will be offered during the house’s Classic Week next year.

The group did not perform particularly well in the end, hammering for a total of just $87.8 million in total, well shy of the low estimate; with the house’s fees, the group sold for $104 million. No lot exceeded its estimate; four fell short of their low estimates. Four of the works sold at an inflation-adjusted loss.

Leading the pack with four works, including the top-estimated piece, was Pablo Picasso; the sale also included examples by Fragonard, Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem, François Le Moyne, Édouard Manet, and Tilman Riemenschneider.

Accounting for up to 60 percent of the total estimate for the sale was Picasso’s Le Baiser (1969), showing two lovers entwined in a kiss and estimated at $40 million–$60 million. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s in 2008 for $17.4 million ($27.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It has hung on the walls of institutions from the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris to London’s National Gallery and New York’s Guggenheim Museum. But the splashy provenance and exhibition history couldn’t get it to its low estimate. It hammered for just $26.5 million to a man bidding in the room, to sell for $31.2 million with the house’s fees.

Picasso’s 1941 canvas Tête de femme (Dora Maar), showing the photographer who was then his lover, was estimated at $25 million–$35 million. Koons acquired it in 2007 at Christie’s New York for $16.3 million ($26.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It barely squeaked by its low estimate to hammer at $25.5 million to the house’s Katharine Arnold, vice-chairman and head of post-war and contemporary art, selling for $30 million million with fees.

He purchased the Spaniard’s Couple (1969), showing a duo in an embrace, at Sotheby’s London in 2011, paying $10.5 million ($15.8 million, adjusted for inflation); it was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. It had not been exhibited since a 1970 show at the Palais des Papes in Avignon, France. It hammered for $13 million to Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, or $15.6 million with fees.

The Spanish artist’s Tête de femme (1939–40) was estimated at $10 million–$15 million. The piece had passed through the hands of the legendary American collectors Burton and Emily Tremaine in the 1940s and the dealer Larry Gagosian in the ’80s. Koons acquired it at Sotheby’s Paris in 2012 for $7.9 million ($11.5 million, adjusted for inflation). It hammered to deputy chairman Olivier Camu for just $6 million, to sell for $7.4 million with fees.

Bound to set a record was the Dutch painter Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem’s 8-foot-wide canvas Hercules and Achelous (1590), which was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. The artist’s previous high was $8.1 million, achieved by the same painting at the same auction house in 2008, when Tuesday’s seller acquired it. It was on loan to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art from then until 2018. That $8.1 million far exceeds the artist’s second-highest price, $1.7 million, set with The Raising of Lazarus (1602) at Christie’s London in 2023. It hammered to Andrew Fletcher, global head of the old masters department, for $11.5 million, just shy of its low estimate, to sell for $13.9 million with fees.

A wooden sculpture by the German artist Tilman Riemenschneider, Saint Catherine (ca. 1505), bore a $4 million–$6 million estimate. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s New York in 2008 for $6.3 million ($10 million, adjusted for inflation), setting the artist’s still-standing record, and then lent it to the Met, where it remained on view until 2019. (That price is double his second-highest, which is, in turn, nearly six times his third-highest.) It hammered within estimate for $4.5 million to François de Poortere, head of old masters for New York, or $5.6 million with fees, shy of what Tuesday night’s seller paid for it.

The cheapest piece on offer from the Koons trove was a Manet pastel, Femme au tub (ca. 1878–79), estimated at $1 million–$1.5 million. Koons paid $2.3 million for it at Sotheby’s London in 2014 ($3.3 million, adjusted for inflation). He lent it to a show that appeared at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Getty and to another at the Met. It hammered shy of the low estimate at $800,000, or $1 million with fees, less than half what the seller paid for it.

Two lasers and a compact size make it ideal for home studios and pop-up event markets.

There's already a lot of competition among the best laser cutters and engravers for crafters, and Creality makes the best budget pick in our guide with its Falcon A1. Today, it's thrown a new contender into the mix, and it looks like it could be a game changer for small personalisation businesses and crafters who want to work remotely.

The next-gen Creality Falcon T1C promises high-performance customisation capabilities, but it's also impressively compact, making it versatile and convenient for things like making custom gifts or adding names, photos, custom text or unique designs to everyday products on location at craft markets and other events (also see our guide to the best 3D printers).

The Falcon T1C is built has a dual-laser configuration that makes it compatible with a wide range of materials. A 15W blue diode laser can process wood, bamboo, leather and dark acrylic, while a 5.5W infrared laser is designed for precision metal marking, dark acrylics and a range of synthetic materials.

Creality says the machine's galvanometer setup (the system that uses motorised mirrors to steer a laser beam) is capable of very fast scan speeds of up to 6,500 mm/s in specified image engraving modes. Using the company's PixelFlow control technology, the system coordinates galvo movement and laser power to preserve fine grayscale details while boosting image-processing efficiency by up to 8x compared to conventional processing under laboratory conditions.

Ultra-fine laser spot sizes (as small as 0.06 x 0.05 mm for the blue diode and 0.03 x 0.03 mm for the infrared laser) promise accurate reproduction for delicate lines, including intricate textures and tiny text, making it possible to personalise very small items.

Aside from the focus on precision, In think what really makes the Falcon T1C a potential game changer is its compact footprint. This makes it an appealing choice for small home studios and workshops but also for anyone who wants to take their customisation business on the move to pop-up event markets. This compactness doesn't necessarily mean sacrificing on potential project size either. The standard 120 x 120 mm working area can be expanded to 120 x 480mm with an optional extension bed for larger items.

One-touch autofocus and camera-assisted positioning should be helpful for speeding up workflows, while the Falcon Design Space software's preset layers eliminate the need to physically swap laser modules or re-align positions, again increasing efficiency for working remotely. It also provides AI Outline Tracing, AI Background Removal, Smart Fill, and AI Filters—to quickly transform design concepts into production-ready physical goods.
