#9037. Christie’s Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt

By Brian Boucher, Harrison Jacobs November 18, 2026 12:22am

At its packed Rockefeller Center saleroom on Tuesday night, Christie’s staged a sometimes lively, sometimes listless two-hour-and-40-minute sale of 20th-century art, led by an $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The house estimated the 74-lot sale to bring $511–$743 million, once adjusted for five works withdrawn before the sale. (Along the withdrawn works was a Frida Kahlo estimated at $2 to $3.5 million, which was pulled just hours before the proceedings were set to begin.) The hammer total for the night came to $521.1 million, slightly above the low estimate. With the house’s fees added, the sale totaled $626.6 million. Related Articles Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso A Wassily Kandinsky Sold by the Nahmads Fetches $85.8 M. at Christie's, Notching a New Auction High

Records were set for Hans Bellmer, Fernando Botero, Wassily Kandinsky, Wifredo Lam, and Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem. At the same time, there were some failures to launch: works by Fernand Léger, Henri Matisse, Joan Mitchell, Amedeo Modigliani, Henry Moore, and Jackson Pollock did not sell. Still, the house found buyers for 68 of the 74 lots offered, for a healthy sell-through rate of 92 percent.

In the room were market players who formed a walking power list. Among them were dealers Jeffrey Deitch, Larry Gagosian, Thaddaeus Ropac, Christophe van de Weghe, and Dominique Lévy and Brett Gorvy, as well as advisors including Amy Cappellazzo, Kim Heirston, Laura Paulson, and Jussi Pylkkänen, formerly the house’s global president. Royalty for the night was David Nahmad, whose family offered the Kandinsky. He sat in his customary spot in the front row and was the underbidder on a few lots, including the Picasso painting Le Baiser, consigned by artist Jeff Koons.

Christie’s equivalent sale last year, which combined selections from the collection of Robert and Patricia Ross Weis with the 20th-century evening sale, totaled a whopping $690 million, making Tuesday’s take 9 percent lower.

Tuesday night’s sale started slow, with the first four lots hammering below estimate, though the last of those, Hans Bellmer’s Jointure de boules (La Poupée), set a new auction record for the artist at $1.67 million with fees. The bidding picked up after that, with a strong showing of in-the-room bidders peppered among the specialists on the phone and a very active online bidder from Florida. Works by Yves Tanguy and Isamu Noguchi hammered well above estimate after spirited bidding, at $4.6 million and $1.2 million, respectively. The Noguchi hammered for double its high estimate; with fees, the price landed at $1.54 million.

That energy carried the crowd well into the star lot of the evening, Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23), which bore a $60–$80 million estimate. Before the sale, the house said the work was guaranteed to set a new record. It sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter; Sara Friedlander, chairman of postwar and contemporary art, Americas; and art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid. With fees, the work landed at $85.8 million, nearly doubling Kandinsky’s previous high of $44.8 million, paid for the artist’s 1910 painting Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) at Sotheby’s London in 2023.

Partway through the sale, DeLuca said of the results, in a text to ARTnews, “The flight to quality is astounding.” That description was as apt for Tuesday’s bidders as it was for DeLuca. He was the underbidder on a number of top lots Tuesday night and lost the Kandinsky by only one bid. (Per the Baer Faxt, De Luca was the winner of the Tanguy.)

To wit, the Claude Monet picture Champ d’avoine et coquelicots, offered three lots later, drew bids from three phone bidders as well as two bidders in the room. That activity sent the painting, which comes from the collection of William I. Koch, soaring past its $12–$18 million estimate. It hammered for $22 million, or $26 million with fees. The Auguste Rodin sculpture Le Penseur, taille de la porte dit “moyen modèle,” offered next and also from the Koch collection, hammered at $6.4 million. With fees, it came to $7.9 million, more than double the high estimate. Another Monet offered later in the sale, La berge du Petit-Gennevilliers, drew the longest bidding of the evening (nine minutes), though one could blame auctioneer Adrien Meyer for some leniency there. Ada Tsui, senior vice president and head of 20th/21st century art for Asia Pacific, and Arco Yu, an associate vice president and specialist who heads the 20th and 21st century art evening sale for Asia Pacific, traded bids in interminable $100,000 increments while they stood shoulder to shoulder, to take the work from a $5 million starting bid to its eventual hammer price of $10.5 million, just a smidge above the $10 million high estimate. With fees, the work’s total came to $12.8 million.

The biggest fireworks came a handful of lots later, when Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915–16) hammered for $71 million after a five-minute contest between Max Carter, the house’s global chairman, and Rotter, who again came away with the prize. The hammer price came smack in the middle of the $60–$80 million estimate, but with fees, it landed at $82.3 million.

By contrast, seven works consigned by Jeff Koons failed to ignite much excitement. The combined low estimate for the group was $104 million, but the hammer total fell shy, at just $87.8 million, with four pieces coming in below their low estimates. With fees, the group totaled, coincidentally, $104 million. The set was led by the Picasso Le Baiser, which hammered at $26.5 million, far below its $40 million low estimate; with fees, the piece brought $31.2 million. A bright spot came with a large canvas by Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem, Hercules and Achelous. Though it hammered for $11.5 million, shy of its $12 million low estimate, it sold for $13.9 million with the house’s fees, setting a new record for the Dutch Old Master. Other works by Picasso, Tilman Riemenschneider, and Édouard Manet filled out the group; see a full report here.

The energy seemed to peter out considerably after the sale of La berge du Petit-Gennevilliers, which followed the Koons trove. Five of the six unsold lots came in the back half of the sale, and 14 of the following 46 lots hammered below estimate. Of the 11 lots in that grouping that overperformed, Diego Rivera’s Vendedora de flores, de Tehuantepec, from the Koch collection, proved the biggest surprise, as four specialists duked it out over seven minutes of bidding before the work hammered for $8.1 million, more than double the $3.5 million high estimate. Sophie Jensen, a client advisory associate, won the contest. The total with fees came to $10 million, within spitting distance of Rivera’s auction record of $14.1 million, set at Christie’s New York in 2022.

Rounding out the night’s top 10 were works by Alberto Giacometti, Henri Matisse, and Mark Rothko. (Noticing a theme here?) The Giacometti, a four-foot-high 1949 bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no. 2), a trademark elongated rendition of a woman, was offered without reserve and with an estimate of $20–$30 million. The collector Herbert Lust had bought it from Chicago collector Joseph R. Shapiro in 1970, and it had been off the market ever since. It hammered for $22 million to a phone bidder via Katharine Arnold, the house’s vice chairman and head of postwar and contemporary art, after a three-minute contest. With fees, the result was $26 million, good for the fifth-best result of the evening.

While it hammered below its $10–$15 million estimate, Wifredo Lam’s Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) did break a record for the artist. After a handful of bids, it hammered for $9.5 million, or $11.6 million with fees. His previous auction record was $9.6 million, set at Sotheby’s New York in 2020. (The winner, again per Baer Faxt, was collector Gary Nader, also the reported winner of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Fist), which sold for $6.2 million with fees.)

Similarly, Fernando Botero’s Horse, the 11-foot-tall rotund bronze sculpture currently residing outside Rockefeller Center, landed within estimate but broke a record for the artist. The work hammered for $4.2 million to a bidder on the phone with Maria Los, deputy chairman and head of client advisory for the Americas. The total with fees of $5.24 million squeaked it past his previous top result of $5.1 million, set at Christie’s in 2023 for the 1979 painting The Musicians.

Tuesday night’s sale was the second of the week, following Sotheby’s two-part Monday night sale, which generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. A sale of works from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum netted $110 million, followed by the house’s Now and Contemporary Art sale, which fetched $268.8 million. Other major sales will follow at Sotheby’s and Christie’s on Wednesday and Thursday nights, respectively.

New York gallerist and art advisor Cristin Tierney put the sale in the context of tech failures at banks, the national air travel system, and even the National Security Agency that plagued the U.S. in the run-up to the sale. “Days and days of software outages, air travel chaos and stock volatility,” she told ARTnews in a text partway through the sale, “but you know what you can count on? Art. Turns out a market based on supporting culture, belief and creativity is the most consistent one of all.”

Advisor Gabriela Palmieri reached for an aviation metaphor to describe the evening. “This week is a congested airspace,” she said in a conversation outside the saleroom. “The houses are doing the most amazing job, because they have to land a lot of planes. There’s incredible elasticity in the market, but the sheer volume of lots is staggering. Anything that fell short, you know, the market is recalibrating. Buyers are drawing the line in certain places. But the houses are achieving a lot of beautiful results.”

#9036. Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The company said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” said Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

“It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler says can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

Most of the electronics are contained on the capsule side, along with a magnetic battery that can be removed for charging outside the bathroom. An accompanying fingerprint scanner is designed to be wall-mounted near the toilet so that users can log in and begin their session.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

Users’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health said Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of new devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

#9035. Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

Adrien Meyer selling Kandinksy's Betonte Ecken (1922-23) for $74m (with fees) at Christie's 20th-century evening sale on 17 November 2026 in New York

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

The hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

The evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustave Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s New York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

French painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590)

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

The Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

The house's total is up 42% from last year's equivalent sale, and it set new auction records for Leonor Fini and Beauford Delaney

The sale was led by a classic 1932 Picasso of Marie-Thérèse at $103.4m and set new records for Alice Neel, Grace Hartigan, Barbara Hepworth and Alighiero Boetti

Last night’s low-risk, low energy auctions made $489m in total, including $272m for the collection of Barnes & Noble founder Leonard Riggio, along with new records for Dorothea Tanning and Remedios Varo

#9034. With a New Miami Partner, Queer Art Prize Returns Following Four-Year Hiatus After Loss of Corporate Support

The Queer Art Prize, the largest cash award in the US for LGBTQ+ artists, is coming back to life after a four-year absence following the loss of corporate support in 2023 that coincided with a wave of anti-trans backlash.

The prize has a new partner in Miami-based gallery Visu Contemporary, which will support the prize’s resurrection. The organization will dole out two $20,000 prizes, one for sustained achievement and one for recent work, double the previous amount. Runners-up for the recent work will each receive $5,000. Related Articles Christie's Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso

In addition to announcing the prize’s return, the nonprofit behind it, Queer | Art, also named the 2026 winner of the Sustained Achievement Award: filmmaker Cheryl Dunye, in recognition of her contributions to Black queer cinema. In her work, Dunye is known to push at the boundaries of filmmaking, with characters addressing the camera and the filmmaker appearing as herself, a genre she has called “Dunyementary.”

The prize comes on the 30th anniversary of her feature film The Watermelon Woman (1996), which won the Teddy Award at the Berlin International Film Festival. She is credited as the first out Black lesbian to ever direct a feature. The Watermelon Woman is widely praised, with Backstage calling it “a landmark indie film.” Her directorial credits also include episodes for television series such as Dear White People, Bridgerton, and Hunting Wives.

With the Sustained Achievement Award, “we want to give people their flowers while they’re still living,” Queer | Art executive director Rio Sofia said in a phone interview. “There are so many moments where we as a community haven’t been able to do that. We lose people too young, so it’s so important to be able to celebrate their hard work and their impact on the culture and the community.”

The winner for the New Work Award will be announced at the organization’s annual party, taking place at Performance Space New York on November 21. The nominees are Jay Carlon (for WAKE, a ritual performance and site-specific dance work), Raquel Gutiérrez (for their debut poetry collection, Southwest Reconstruction), Ashley Teamer (for Portal Work, an immersive installation), and Dorian Wood (for Canto de Todes, a musical composition). The emcee for the evening will be writer, comedian, and performance artist Erin Markey, whose stage presence was once described by a director as “very alien, like Barbie from outer space.”

The prize’s new partner, Visu Contemporary, is located just a few hundred feet from the Bass Museum of Art and a few blocks from the Miami Beach Convention Center. Under owner and curator Bruce Halpryn, the gallery has shown artists like Barry X. Ball, David LaChapelle, and Dustin Yellin. Annual public programming will spotlight artists from the Queer | Art community, including prize winners and finalists. A future exhibition of Queer Art Prize winners will take place in 2027.

Founded in 2009, Queer | Art provides intergenerational mentorship, public programming, and material support for LGBTQ+ artists. The organization hopes to create some of the intergenerational connection, particularly mentorship, that has been devastated by the ongoing AIDS pandemic. The Queer Art Prize was inaugurated in 2017 and continued until 2022, supported by HBO, which then abruptly withdrew its sponsorship. HBO did not respond to emails from ARTnews requesting comment about the end of its support.

In 2023, various companies in the US saw a rash of controversy for marketing themselves to queer communities. When Bud Light ran a social media promotion including transgender actress Dylvan Mulvaney, some boycotted the brand; Trump-aligned entertainer Kid Rock filmed himself shooting cases of the drink with a submachine gun. Retailer Target saw sales decline after it offered LGBTQ+ merchandise during Pride month that year. Companies like Calvin Klein, Glamour, Adidas, and the North Face came in for similar backlash for highlighting trans people. At the same time, at least nine GOP-led state legislatures moved to restrict or even criminalize drag shows.

Sofia, Queer | Art’s director, said HBO wasn’t the only one to part ways with the nonprofit: The organization lost all its corporate funding, some $200,000, in the same period. Under the Trump administration, it has also lost government funding that it previously received.

The Queer Art Prize returns at a moment when the American political establishment could hardly be said to have warmed to LGBTQ+ people, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even using a slur to refer to transgender people in a recent speech and the Trump administration adopting the official position that there are only two genders, denying the existence of transgender people.

While some organizations may have recently toned down their messaging to avoid controversy, Sofia said, “We are the Queer Art Prize! So there’s no hiding what we do. Our approach has been to double down on both the size of the organization and our capacity.”

Doubling the prizes and giving cash to the runners-up, she said, “sends a really clear message about what we’re about and the kind of defiance that is part of the roots of an organization that was founded by ACT UP members.”

In a statement, Visu’s Halpryn said, “Supporting Queer|Art in establishing these prizes is not philanthropy—it’s cultural authorship at a moment when visibility itself is contested. LGBTQIA+ artists have shaped the trajectory of contemporary art for decades, yet too often without proportional recognition or institutional backing. As a gay curator, I believe that acknowledging both lifetime achievement and new work is essential to correcting that imbalance and defining what comes next.”

Halpryn added, “This partnership is designed not just to honor artists, but to place their work in sustained dialogue with collectors, curators, and the public. If we care about the future of culture, we have to be deliberate about whose voices we elevate—and whose histories we refuse to let disappear.”

Online sleuths think they've found the answer.

Prince George made the headlines recently by displaying his artistic flair. The second in line to the throne impressed readers of Country Life magazine last week, when his colour pencil drawing of a kingfisher appeared in a special issue guest edited by his father, the Prince of Wales.

Shortly afterwards, the drawing went viral and amazed audiences on social media as well. It’s not hard to see why. The bird, which is playfully perched on a little branch and looking away from the viewer, demonstrates a level of craft you might not expect to come from the hands of a 12-year-old.

If you wish you could draw this well, and you’ve exhausted all of our how to draw tutorials, you might be in luck. Because shrewd online detectives may have figured out the secret behind the Prince’s handiwork.

Upon being shared on the likes of X and Instagram, people couldn’t believe how good the drawing was. Some commenters pointed out that he may have inherited his artistic talent from his family. After all, Prince George’s grandfather, King Charles, is an avid watercolour painter, and his parents both studied art at A-level. Catherine even studied history of art while at university.

The internet being what it is though, it wasn’t long until jealous users credited the drawing’s success to the amount of time and extra tuition the Prince surely enjoyed. However it seems he may have simply followed an easily accessible online course.

In amongst the comments, it soon became apparent that Prince George’s drawing bears more than a passing resemblance to the kingfisher featured in Matt Fussell’s course titled 3 Little Birds. And while no official confirmation has been made at the time of writing, everything from the pose to the positioning on the branch appears to be very similar.

This isn’t to take away from the Prince’s drawing. His picture still showcases a great level of skill and a keen understanding of the materials. In this case, if he followed the tutorial to the letter, Prince George used wax-based Prismacolor Premier Pencils on smooth Bristol paper. Both of which can be easily picked up from most local art supply shops.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

If anything, it should be an encouragement to aspiring artists. With the help of one course, which can be enjoyed as either videos or step-by-step written instructions, you too can start layering your colours and creating your own beautiful bird illustrations (see our how to draw a bird tutorial, for example).

According to the course outline on his website, Matt’s instructions make the drawing process easy by breaking everything down into simple lessons. These cover everything from the proportions to colour transitions, as well as texture and highlights. Follow the course through to the end, and you’ll also learn how to draw a blue jay with oil-based polychroma pencils by Faber Castell, and a hummingbird with wax-based luminance coloured-pencils from Caran D’Ache.

On top of helping you draw like Prince George, these are also useful skills that can be carried over into future studies. And if you’re not happy with your results, Matt even offers a 30 day money back guarantee on his $57 course.

Dom Carter is a freelance writer who specialises in art and design. Formerly a staff writer for Creative Bloq, his work has also appeared on Creative Boom and in the pages of ImagineFX, Computer Arts, 3D World, and .net. He has been a D&AD New Blood judge, and has a particular interest in picture books.

#9032. Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a new public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a new quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” said Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”

The retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” said Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

TERROR’S TREASURY. The British Council has provided public funding to the Palestinian Museum in Birzeit, West Bank, which has been accused of glorifying terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians, The Telegraph reports. Exhibits include posters depicting Dalal al-Mughrabi, who led the 1978 Coastal Road massacre in which 38 Israelis were killed, as a martyr, alongside material celebrating Hamas bomb-maker Yahya Ayyash. UK Lawyers for Israel has called for funding to be suspended and an investigation launched. The Charity Commission has opened a regulatory compliance case into Taawon UK, a charity linked to the museum. The British Council says it is reviewing the allegations, while Taawon denies wrongdoing. Related Articles Sotheby's $180 M. Van Gogh Sale Faces Nazi-Era Restitution Claim, What Happened to Lucas Museum's Educational Programming? and More: Morning Links for November 16, 2026 Microsoft Outage Disrupts Global Operations and Art World Too, Undercover Investigation Busts Fake UK Artist Visas, and More: Morning Links for November 13, 2026

TEPID RESULT AT CHRISTIE’S. As ARTnews reported, Christie’s 20th-century art evening sale at Rockefeller Center raised $626.6 million including fees. The 74-lot auction was led by a Wassily Kandinsky abstraction, which sold for $85.8 million, followed by a Gustav Klimt landscape at $82.3 million. The sale’s hammer total was $521.1 million, just above the low estimate. Five works were withdrawn before the auction, including a Frida Kahlo painting estimated at $2–3.5 million, which was pulled just hours before proceedings began.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews has launched a new £15,000 contemporary art prize to support artists creating work inspired by Jewish culture, heritage, and tradition. [Jewish News]

The UK government has placed an export ban on Mughal calligraphy works valued at £900,000 and delayed the export of an 18th-century marble bust of Edward the Black Prince, to give a British museum the opportunity to acquire it. [UK Gov]Harvard’s Peabody Museum has returned the remains of a man and woman, believed to have been enslaved, to Brazil after more than 150 years in its collection. [The Art Newspaper]Simon O’Donovan, a National Museum of Ireland staffer charged with possessing an improvised explosive device, is seeking the return of his car and other property seized by the police. [Irish Times]

COLLECTING DUST. A dinosaur fossil that sat in a drawer at London’s Natural History Museum for nearly a century has been identified as a previously unknown species, Futura reports. Named Invictibellatrix amberina, it’s the first megaraptoran discovered in Europe. The three-to-four-metre-long predator lived around 120 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous period and was closely related to tyrannosaurs. Its skull fragment was acquired by the museum in 1924, having been discovered on the Isle of Wight by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley. Researchers say the long-clawed, feathered dinosaur would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards, and mammals.

It's clear that some people are getting tired of the contemporary Disney style. That can be seen in the allegations of Disney same-face syndrome, the disappointment that Hexed doesn't look like its concept art and the perennial controversy over the hybrid live-action remakes, with Moana being the latest flop.

The fatigue was evident at D23 this year. The announcements that generated the most excitement were a return of 2D animation, if only in combination with live action for the nostalgia-heavy TV series in Oswald, and the news that Disney's Clay will look like claymation even if uses CG.

A lot of fans will be happy then to learn that Clay won't be a one off but rather the start of a whole new Disney era after Hexed. The studio's developed a new animation pipeline that will allow it to apply different art styles to 3D models, potentially replacing the realism popularised by Pixar with a unique look for each new movie – and it's all starting with Lilo & Scratch.

Set to show in cinemas alongside Hexed, Lilo & Scratch is the first theatrical short from Walt Disney Animation Studios in five years. Written and directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Malcon Pierce, it will see the much-loved blue alien Stitch having to contend with the introduction of a mischievous cat called Scratch. Maia Kealoha voices Lilo, reprising her role from the 2025 live-action film Lilo & Stitch, and Chris Sanders with voice Stitch again.

Like all of the studios' feature animations in the last 15 years, the short was made using computer-generated animation with 3D models, but these are blended with hand-drawn elements to create a hybrid style that looks surprisingly faithful to Lilo & Stitch from 2002.

Disney's VFX supervisor Jeremy Sikorski has said that the new pipeline was developed through experimentation on the previous shorts Paperman and Once Upon a Studio. Pixar is also exploring the same direction, as we saw in the Gatto trailer: environments, characters and sets are modeled and animated in 3D to retain spatial depth, lighting and camera movement, but certain characters and other details are hand drawn.

Disney says about 25% of the backgrounds in Lilo & Scratch are watercolour paintings reused from the original Lilo & Stitch, while more than a dozen new background paintings were created by artists including Tia Kratter and Larry Wu. Some of these were digitally painted in Photoshop to look like watercolour, while others were hand-painted on paper.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Combined with digital backgrounds and set extension, this blend of old and new hand-painted watercolours helped the filmmakers remain faithful to the look of the 2002 feature, Disney says.

In an interview at the Governors Awards in LA on Sunday (see the post by Deadline below), Disney Animation Chief Creative Officer Jared Bush confirmed that all original Disney movies from Clay onwards will use this approach. That doesn't mean that they'll all look like Renaissance-era 2D animation, but that each with have its own "wildly different" look.

Zootopia 3 and Frozen 3 will still look like we would expect, but Hexed may be "the last original in the Disney art style as people know it," he says.

Jared Bush shares updates on ‘Zootopia 3,’ ‘Frozen 3’ and ‘Hexed’ and reveals the new, upcoming animated films at Disney will have “wildly different art styles”: “We’re really going to be pushing into some new areas” | #GovernorsAwards https://t.co/nw16Ci8WoDNovember 16, 2026

The new approach looks like a win for Disney. Despite some success with the live-action The Jungle Book and last year's Lilo & Stitch, the poor reception of Moana, Snow White and Mulan suggests waning interest in the remake formula is waning. Meanwhile, the 3D animation style that once looked so modern is starting to feel dated and generic.

Nostalgic audiences miss 2D animation, while younger audiences want something fresh. It sounds like Disney's new animation pipeline could make both things possible without sacrificing the efficiency that comes with 3D-based CG animation, which makes it much quicker and easier to swap and adjust environments, characters and props compared to traditional hand-drawn 2D, where even a relatively small change might mean having to redraw from scratch.The Disney principles of animation will remain in tact, but in a vast realm new possibilities.

I do wonder though. In ten years time, will people start to feel nostalgic about the much-maligned 3D Disney style?

Hexed will be released on 25 November. Lilo & Scratch will screen before it.

#9029. MoMA Plans First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Nearly 25 Years for 2027

Following an acclaimed retrospective at Tate Modern in London, Ana Mendieta will be the subject of yet another super-sized show, this one staged across the pond, at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, where it will run from December 12, 2027, to April 16, 2028.

MoMA’s Mendieta show, titled simply “Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective,” will include around 200 works by the artist, an icon of the feminist art movement, a key performance artist, and a sculptor and filmmaker whose work in those mediums has only increased in popularity over the past couple decades. That makes the show the biggest Mendieta exhibition ever staged in the US, where the Cuban-born artist spent much of her short career. Related Articles MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for 'Nature-Reconciled' Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA's West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It

It’s the first major Mendieta show in the US since one staged in 2004 by curator Olga Viso for the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, and the first full-scale Mendieta retrospective mounted in the country since one visited the New Museum in New York in 1987, when the artist was less well-known than she is now. A survey focused solely on Mendieta’s films visited various US institutions in 2016.

But where past Mendieta shows have largely been thematic or centered around her output in a specific medium, the MoMA show is intended as a comprehensive retrospective.

Beverly Adams and Sophie Cavoulacos, the MoMA curators organizing the exhibition, said in an email to ARTnews, “First, and foremost, Ana Mendieta is a great artist, truly brilliant. Beyond making compelling images and objects, the issues that were of interest to her continue to be relevant today. Mendieta expanded many of the debates around performance, feminism, photography, and earth art in the 1970s and early 1980s. She investigated a body’s relationship with nature, with place and how an artist can explore a single idea through different mediums.”

One goal of the show, they said, is to demonstrate that Mendieta’s work in many mediums allowed her to translate and retranslate ideas. “She would craft how her remote environmental sculptures would be experienced in film and photographs,” the curators wrote. “Throughout the show, we are interested in elevating Mendieta’s process and how the different mediums she worked with resonate with each other.”

By way of example, the curators cited Mendieta’s paintings made while she was a student at the University of Iowa. These works have never before been shown in the US, the curators said, and they are “a point of departure for what was to follow.”

Much of Mendieta’s work dealt with the female body, which she explored as a site of violence, a vessel for the spirit world, and a parallel for nature and the environment. During the 1970s and ’80s, she built up an impressive, and occasionally transgressive, oeuvre that touched on topics such as rape, diasporic identity, and gendered power dynamics—all subjects that many mainstream museums generally would not feature in their galleries when she made these pieces.

Her most famous works remain the ones in her “Silueta” series (1973–85), for which she created the silhouettes of female forms in nature. To create the early works in the series, Mendieta pressed her body into landscapes across Mexico and Iowa, then used mud, sand, fire, and flowers to record her impression, and finally documented what was left behind with her camera. She would go on to make sculptures that recall these silhouettes; they were produced at roughly the scale of her body.

Among Adams’s recent shows for MoMA was a 2025 Wifredo Lam retrospective that placed an emphasis on the role that the artist’s Cuban identity played in his work. The Mendieta show will seemingly function somewhat differently.

“Mendieta was born in Cuba, but lived the majority of her life in the United States and identified as someone coming from both of these cultures,” Adams and Cavoulacos said in their joint statement. “She went to art school in Iowa and moved to New York where she bridged different communities. She was initially propelled to make art by her exile and displacement from Cuba, but her work transcended the idea of nation-based identity.”

Mendieta’s death at the age of 36 in 1985, caused by falling from the window of the New York apartment she shared with her partner, the sculptor Carl Andre, has long troubled the telling of her story for curators, art historians, and fans alike. Andre was tried for murder and was subsequently acquitted in 1988. Andre’s death at the age of 88 in 2024 spurred newfound interest in the circumstances of Mendieta’s death, which was the subject of a podcast by the curator Helen Molesworth two years earlier.

Mendieta’s estate, which will lend works to the MoMA retrospective, has attempted to discourage reading the artist through the lens of her death. Raquel Cecilia Mendieta, the artist’s goddaughter and the manager of the estate, asked in 2014, in the New York Times: “How many times does she have to fall?” According to the New Yorker, ahead of the Tate Modern retrospective, Mendieta’s estate began circulating a document called “FACT SHEET” that asserts that the artist’s death is “not remotely related to how she created her art, nor was her art predestined or shaped by her death in any way, shape or form.”

Tate Modern’s current retrospective omits mention of Mendieta’s death, which led critic Eliza Goodpasture to write, in her Art in America review: “This exhibition is a proposition: What does Mendieta’s work become if we allow it to stand on its own?”

Asked whether Mendieta’s death would be explored in MoMA’s exhibition, Adams and Cavoulacos said, “Our role as curators organizing a comprehensive retrospective is to focus on the artist’s career and celebrate her immense contributions to art history.”

#9027. Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

Normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online. A new logo can draw furious ire, as brands like Jaguar and Cracker Barrel have discovered in recent years. Less controversial tends to be copywriting tweaks. But beauty brand Maybelline's 'new' slogan has infuriated me more. Than. Any. Other. Rebrand. This. Year.

“Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline," was one of the most famous jingles on TV for a while. It first debuted in the 1990s (see the original below), and is burned onto the consciousness of countless viewers. But now, in a attempt to remove its so-called "ambiguity", the slogan has been updated. Nay, butchered. One of the best pieces of copywriting, this ain't.

The new slogan reads: "Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline." Yes, "she's" has been changed to a more inclusive "we're". But it's that stuttering punctuation that's bothering me. Why does it suddenly sound like it's being recited by somebody struggling to walk up a hill?

According to Sandrine Jolly, Maybelline's global brand president, the original jingle "was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question". Well, yes. That was rather the point. The word 'Maybe' is, by its very nature, an ambiguous word. Its synonyms include 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. Its entire meaning is uncertainty. You can't change that by giving it a full stop. Trying to remove the ambiguity from a slogan built entirely around ambiguity is a bit like changing Nike's 'Just Do It' to 'Please. Consider. Doing. It.'

And there's nothing wrong with changing 'she' to 'we'. It's a perfectly reasonable attempt at inclusivity, and one that could have been achieved without completely murdering the rhythm. Instead, Maybelline has taken one of the catchiest jingles of all time and made it sound like a hostage reading out a statement. Four sentences where there used to be two. Does that really make for more certainty?

What makes it all so infuriating is that this feels like change for change's sake. The original slogan was clever, memorable and instantly recognisable. The new one needs an entire press release to explain what its punctuation represents. In an era when brands are realising the importance of their heritage branding assets, maybe, just maybe, Maybelline should have left its slogan. Alone.

#9025. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

#9024. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

#9023. Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.
