#9003. Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”

Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

“Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”

Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” said Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”

Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

“One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”

History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between researchers Hiba Bou Akar and Mohamad Hafeda and artist Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

“We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”

After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”

Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.

Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani

Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Is it a step too far for virtual branding?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best NHL logos are timeless, but the National Hockey League has been covering them up recently, at least on television broadcasts. After the addition of dynamic digital advertising on dashers and on the ice, the league's latest technological 'advance' is the use of digital overlays to replace real centre logos with temporary virtual ones.

Spectators in the arena see the home team's usual design, but viewers watching on TV are shown the team's Hometown Remix logo, a temporary alternate design being used for select games. It must have seemed like a great idea when it was floated, but it doesn't seem to be going down well with viewers, with some saying they'll stop watching if the practice continues.

@The_Mexinadian There’s already too much virtual crap on the ice and video as it is. Why do we need a HUGE fake logo that hurts my eyes whenever anyone skates over it?!November 15, 2026

Hometown Remix is a leaguewide campaign in which each team has a special-edition uniform featuring specifically local references. Many teams are using modified, throwback or entirely redesigned logos. The NHL says the campaign "uniquely and authentically celebrates the fans, fabric, and local culture of each NHL team and the cities they call home".

But in sports like the NHL, a logo design isn't just an identity, it's revenue. Multiple logos, throwback designs and temporary remixes all largely about selling a new range of merchandise. Putting a temporary logo on the ice becomes highly visible advertising for alternate jerseys. The problem is that it's appalling to look at.

The ice is *the* thing that immediately separates watching hockey from watching any other sport the instant you turn it on. It's beautiful and unique. Slapping giant fake digital novelty logos on top of the earnestly painted logos that are actually there is a shame. https://t.co/JvoXxCJWkONovember 13, 2026

You can literally see a white glow around every player at center ice??? How was this approvedNovember 18, 2026

WHAT IS THE POINT!?!?! https://t.co/GLRkQI5M30November 15, 2026

Some viewers already complained about the digitisation of adverts on dashers and on the ice to make them look more prominent. For some, the new virtual logos is the last straw, making the viewing experience feel detached from reality.

The lack of motion blur or shadows on the digital fake when players pass over the centre of the ice makes it look uncanny, as though players are passing in front of a badly keyed green screen. Any black in the design can make the puck momentarily disappear from view.

"When they brought in the digitally superimposed ads on the boards I stopped watching altogether. Too distracting and horribly done. I remember seeing players disappear into the ads," one person writes on X.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Some fans are concerned that the NHL's use of virtual team logos could be merely the start and that the league might be testing the ground to potentially replace team logos with sponsors. I'm not sure brands would want to be associated with the backlash that would cause.

Designers have to consider an increasingly wide range of potential digital applications for logo designs these days. On the ice in an NHL game probably shouldn't be one of them.

#9001. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Research shows that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo says. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”

#9000. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#8999. GTA 6 review: Holy sh*t it’s good

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Funny, sad, euphoric… GTA 6 is the most entertaining and emotionally engaging open world I’ve played. Rockstar has taken the sandbox freedom of Grand Theft Auto and the environmental storytelling of Red Dead Redemption 2 and made something that feels lived-in. The characters, humour, and systems are all wonderfully written, and the attention to detail makes Leonida a place I want to stay in long after I’d finished the story. The set pieces rival Hollywood, but I'll remember the small, unplanned moments.

An extraordinarily detailed, living open world

Jason and Lucia are brilliant protagonists

Hilarious, unpredictable emergent gameplay

Superb environmental storytelling and art direction

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In brief: 5/5. Grand Theft Auto VI (reviewed on PS5, out 19 November) is the most convincing open world I’ve played.

I laughed out loud multiple times within minutes of starting Grand Theft Auto VI. Not a chuckle or a smirk, but proper laughs, grinning ear to ear, as a particularly large resident of Leonida giggled, ran, stumbled, staggered and tripped over a railing into the river below. It was ridiculous and completely unexpected, and I loved it.

We've waited 13 years for GTA VI and from the opening credits, Rockstar has crafted a hyperreal but intensely personal world where every corner of Leonida and Vice City offers a surprise. I've been playing for three weeks, finished the story, seen some endings, and I'm still playing to find out what random secrets Leonida has left to share. Much of it has nothing to do with the fate of Lucia and Jason, GTA VI's modern-day Bonnie and Clyde. (Read our GTA VI coverage for more on the game.)

Driving around, you'll spot Just Stop Oil-style protests blocking traffic, teenagers dropping rocks onto motorway cars, or posters and flyers that lead to mysteries and new characters to call from your iFruit phone's contacts list. These aren't side quests in the traditional sense, with a marker on your map and a list to tick off; they're connections to random people, and the sense that this world exists beyond the screen.

Those teenagers dropping rocks? I detoured to teach them a lesson. Later, I stopped for someone posting for social media while balancing on a bridge, and failed to save him when he fell, and I actually felt bad. I pulled over for some teens daring each other to jump from a bridge into a river, decided to show them how it was done, and while I was swimming, they stole my car.

It's not risk and reward; it's just life in Leonida. It's incredibly fun.

The scale of GTA VI is incredible, but not in the usual sense of a vast map to cross. It's the depth and detail that gets me: the branding, signage, store shelves of snacks and comic books that can be read, snatches of conversations from passersby muttering about their lives or something they heard on the radio, the same thing I heard on the radio. Most buildings can be broken into and explored, and I've spent far too long sneaking into warehouses that have no obvious reason to exist beyond making the world feel authentic and the possibility that something of value could be snaffled away inside.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Shops, bars and clubs are lovingly detailed, and once inside you're free to toy with the world. Buy something, drink something for a stat bonus, steal something, change your clothes, or earwig and people watch. Sometimes you'll need to change outfits, because it throws off the cops chasing you; sometimes just because you feel you should wear beach clothes on the beach, because I'm completely hooked into this world.

The geography is considered too. Vice City is a maze of overpasses and winding spaghetti motorway junctions; the city itself is a muddle of back alleys, malls, and beachfront hotels, while the roads out in the country are simpler and more relaxed; the swamps need care to navigate; the sandy, wooded isles of the north are a stolen boat. Beaches, swamps, forests and distinct neighbourhoods all have their own character, and you feel it: stressed in Vice City, calm and playful up north, the mullet of map design, if you will. Even the residents and police behave differently depending on where you are.

Early on, Jason and Lucia visit a rich, enclaved community filled with jewellery shops, polished pavements and high-fashion stores practically demanding to be robbed. A policeman on a bicycle stops them and warns them that their kind isn't welcome. I pushed my luck, choosing confrontational dialogue options, refused to obey, and he called in backup from other pedal-bike cops who made it clear our kind wasn't welcome. I returned at night and stole everything, and it felt so good.

Giving you an emotional reason to do things is one of GTA VI's biggest successes. You start to understand the people who live here, the divisions between communities and the little injustices that make you want to cause trouble.

There's always something happening, too. An armoured car is robbed, so I follow it to the thieves' hideout and steal everything. A farm sign says 'pilot wanted', so I drop in and end up in a whole side story about meth-strawberries that eventually riffs on a Marvel character I never expected. Leonida's residents are 'Karens on crack', too. Scrape someone's car, and they'll chase you down; look at someone too long, and they'll demand a fight; drive down a motorway, and hyped up teen will lean out of their car to challenge you to a race. Once I planned a bank heist, only to find a random gang shooting the place up, and I got caught in the melee. It's layer upon layer of random, living events, and even on a mission, it's easy to get sidetracked as gunshots ring out.

GTA VI rewards your downtime too; it wants you to simply enjoy the place and the moment because conversations eavesdropped on in a bar are hilarious but also tease secrets about the world, whether residents are complaining about the weather or arguing over culture-war nonsense raised by the State's shock jock, who is furious about that weekend's Manatees football result and the demise of 'mansculinity'. Some can be engaged with and will share random but useful news about Leonida.

There's no Ubisoft-style checklist here. Stunts, hidden collectable cards (which you can sell in-game), fishing challenges and sporting events are there if you want them, but the world grows as you explore, meet people and build up your contacts list. You just exist in Leonida and enjoy exploring, competing and completing things.

The weather is a big part of that experience, because it looks beautiful – golden morning sunlight cuts through thick mist over a wildflower meadow with realism, dramatic storm clouds and dense golden fog engulf a city skyline, obscuring buildings and bridges in an atmospheric haze.

But weather also affects how you engage with the world. Days feel long enough to play in, different things happen at different times, and the weather is dramatic and distinct. That hazy mist can obscure your visibility, while hard rain can limit distance and disrupt sound, something used to dramatic effect in a nighttime kidnapping rescue where large halogen lights pierced the rain and mist, creating drama but affecting line of sight in some spaces.

Likewise, a plane handles differently in wind, rain and cloud, as the controls judder and inputs feel less responsive. Flying through a storm, with lightning sparking and rolling across the horizon, gives you a real sense of place and moment but also puts you slightly on edge.

Jason and Lucia's relationship really surprised me in GTA VI, and it's one area where Rockstar picks up where Red Dead Redemption 2 left off. Both are well-rounded protagonists with motivations and shared dreams that you help build. Lucia is alive and sprightly, Jason is dour and determined, and how their connection develops, or doesn't, becomes a game of its own.

A subtle romance and empathy system is at play. How much time the pair spend together, the conversations you choose, the dates, time at home (yes, you can make love in the shower, on the sofa, in the kitchen and, well, all sorts of places) and even how and when you plan and commit crimes all feed into how their relationship develops, and it can affect how their story ends.

What you do on a job matters too. Kill lots of people, and you get a different criminal rating than if you spare lives, and the duo seem to have a healthier relationship if you play to control a room with threats or shoot to injure rather than murder. I wanted a loving crime couple, so almost without meaning to, I started shooting people in the legs and arms to make them fall or drop their guns instead of headshotting everyone in a room. I wanted my Lucia to like my Jason.

Likewise, when Jason went undercover as 'the poolboy' for a saucy film shoot, I held back on how far I took things. Lucia was getting madder in my ear as Jason applied lotion to an actress, and when given the choice to go all in, as it were, I pulled out, as they say, as it were, because I wanted Lucia to still like Jason. I still don't know how far you can take that mission, but this is Rockstar, so I imagine it's all the way (and that's what she said).

Few games get that emotional connection right. It doesn't come only from good writing and characterisation, but from all the little conversations, actions, reactions and animated moments when they meet up or succeed. You'd have a heart of stone to go out of your way to ruin their romance, because you can. You monster.

Controlling when and how they meet up is part of GTA V's character-switching development. Moving between them is nearly instantaneous: the camera pulls out to a global view, zooms back down, and you can message the other to hook up or tell them to meet you somewhere. And you do get committed: when I occasionally Irish-goodbye'd Jason, I felt the need to call him and check up.

The central narrative picks up what worked in Red Dead Redemption 2, splitting the story into chapters that each introduce a new gang or cast and a grand setup to plan towards. The structure gives you plenty to play with, and the story spans more years as the couple bounces from backwater crimes to epic, militarised heists. These feed into cinematic tentpole moments that draw on everything from the later Fast and Furious movies to Assault on Precinct 13, with even a little nod to Die Hard as Lucia sparks a lighter in an air vent, laughs and paraphrases the classic line, "Come out to the coast, we'll get together, have a few laughs."

It's also where Rockstar's love of a good heist movie really shines. Some of the bigger set pieces have the clockwork precision of an Edgar Wright film, with different characters, objectives and moving parts all working towards one carefully choreographed finale. The editing is part of the fun: the action cuts between Jason and Lucia as they tackle their separate jobs, each sequence dovetailing with the next as the plan unfolds, the clock ticks down, and the stakes rise.

The grand finales of each chapter are proper spectacles that never play out the same way and deliver 'cinema'. You might be flying gunships over a stormy ocean, or swapping between Jason and Lucia as they complete different parts of a larger plan. Jason races to a rooftop to stop mobster reinforcements while Lucia hacks a vault, and you're jumping between the two as the action cuts back and forth, the tempo building with each switch. One moment you're holding off a gang; the next, you're working through the other side of the operation, and it all clicks together like clockwork. It's a wonderfully cinematic way to make character switching part of the action, not just a convenient way to get around the map.

Around these set pieces that take time to build are lower-key missions, some tailored to each character, and this is where Rockstar earns its rewards. The satire of modern America, social media, celebrity culture and consumerism that we love about GTA is here in abundance. A favourite is a storyline in which Lucia becomes embroiled in a bored-housewives vape cult that's like Goop meets Elizabeth Holmes.

Then there are the random encounters that make Leonida feel active, and never run how you think. An elderly woman screaming for help on a back road took me to her farmhouse, where I expected a robbery or a rescue. Instead, a client had 'died' in a bondage orgy gone wrong, and I needed to dispose of the body in a river. Even that didn't end as I expected.

Even 40-plus hours into the main story, Rockstar finds new ways to surprise me. It introduces a vault-hacking mini-game that uses haptics and controller prompts for one bank job, then drops in a drug-dog sidekick for a single mission. Ideas are picked up, enjoyed and dropped before they go stale. GTA VI has so many that it never has to hang around with one for long.

Shooting and weapon handling are superb, and each gun feels distinct. The cover system and enemy AI respond nicely even in busy rooms, and stealth is reliable and effective. While the big set-piece story missions can feel a little restrictive and scripted because they need to reach the cinematic heights Rockstar is aiming for, anything can happen outside them.

A bank heist, for example, needs proper planning. Park a getaway car, choose the right vehicle, pick the rear door lock, hack the cameras, wear a disguise, and don't overstay your welcome. The world is so well designed and systematised that everything feels connected. Next time, go in through the front door, or steal a truck and pull an ATM from the wall. Heists in backwater towns are easier because there are fewer police around. And nothing plays out quite as you expect; every bank is unique, and after two seamless jobs I go for a third and it all goes wrong – an unexpected teller wanders into the office for a coffee, an alarm is tripped, and before I realise it, I'm shooting my way out, bags shouldered, and looking for a new car to steal… the best-laid plans are shot.

The police react to all this more deeply than in previous GTAs. There's no longer just a star rating and a zone to escape, but how you escape matters. Swap cars and clothes, and they'll lose you, because they're looking for your description, not you, me, the player. All the old tricks are still here, from roadblocks and air support to increasingly aggressive police AI, but you have new ways to shake them off beyond just driving fast.

It ties into car ownership too, another Red Dead Redemption 2 influence. You can't carry everything, so it's worth stowing a change of clothes and weapons in your car. Carrying a gun openly gets the police involved, but some Vice City passers-by will also decide to take you out as well.

Driving feels familiar from GTA V, but with enough nuance to feel like an evolution, as cars have different weights and handling, and each one reacts differently through the DualSense triggers: sports cars resist less than family saloons when you pull to accelerate. Boats, bikes, planes and helicopters all work as you'd expect, but even here there are subtle shifts in how responsive each can be – one helicopter I stole was uncontrollable and spun into the swamp.

Character models, facial animation, skin, hair, and clothing all deliver the hyperrealism I expected from a new GTA, though they're still larger-than-life caricatures built to feel relatable rather than photorealistic.

Animation, including the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes, is where GTA VI takes its biggest strides. Lucia and Jason are wonderfully handled, whether it's the little snuggles and embraces or the way they hold up a bank and play off one another, but the breadth of animation across GTA VI is what impresses. Every Leonida resident feels uniquely animated, and it's fun just to people-watch. Early on, a drunk girl follows Jason around a bar and is authentically annoying, and the nightlife feels realistically overwhelming. Bar bands are animated to sell their next song, and even the wildlife has moments: I watched a white-tailed doe and buck nuzzle each other lovingly and naturally through Jason's rifle scope. It was cute enough to make me take a breath, but Jason needs more money, so the shot rang out and the wildlife scattered.

Leonida has a recognisable visual identity, bold and vibrant, with every corner full of quirks, from the deep forests of the north to the out-of-town mall and rows of copy-and-paste suburban houses. Fictional adverts, billboards, shops, signage, and TV build the world, as if you see an ad for a beer or car, and you can buy it (or steal it). Beyond signage, graffiti walls, sculptures, exhibits, and more invite you to linger and just take in the world.

It also feels like a realistic evolution of the 1980s Vice City I knew and loved, a city with a history inside a broader world, with references to Liberty City aplenty, from car number plates to Jason and Lucia's accents. It's somewhere to wallow, whether you're having a cocktail under palm trees swaying in a breeze or tearing up Vice City in a neon-lit supercar while crypto bros trade and wannabe rappers parade.

It's a wonder this all runs on a base PS5. I remember the mess of equally ambitious games like Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, but GTA VI is in a different league. The frame rate is locked at 30fps, and it's fine: stable, with little slowdown or stutter, and controls and handling feel spot on. There's occasional soft pop-in, but few visual compromises or trip-ups. You can feel the work that's gone into making everything run smoothly, and GTA 6 is polished to perfection.

I'm really only scratching the surface. Familiar street races, bank heists, and chilled fishing and hunting trips are joined by crypto rug pulls, golf tournaments, and deep-sea treasure hunts. Or I just drive, hunt a swamp thing, stop to solve a mystery from a local ad, or relax with a game of pool and a Patriot beer. You can take on the State's sports and races, go sailing, or listen to 80s FM hits, the biggest dance tracks, or to the MAGA-inspired Richard Bastion Show – "more volume than logic" – who's mad about everything.

This game has video games inside it that feel more complete than some real games I've played, from the top-down sci-fi shooter Time Jackers: Rewind to a lightgun score-chasing bar game Bang For Your Buck. And in typical Rockstar fashion, they all have a satirical edge, like the indie auteur game Tenebrae Lux, which pokes fun at the po-faced walking sims that were all the rage: it's black-and-white, minimal, and filled with overwritten prose like a Taylor Swift song about metaphors.

GTA VI is a world that exists beyond its main story, where everything feeds into and off each other. It's the best world-building I've experienced in a game in years, partly because its systems all work in a coherent, purposeful and layered way, but also because it's not afraid to be weird, whether that's discovering the dumpster lawyer, becoming a frog, slobbing on the sofa and watching an episode of Whose Dick's Whose, or finding an influencer in the boot of a stolen car who wants to be kidnapped for clout.

There are minor restrictions, mainly when the big cinematic missions take over and funnel you down a more scripted path, but for good reason, and the 30fps cap won't suit everyone (yet it's really not an issue). But in a game that otherwise gives you this much freedom, they're the exception.

13 years? The wait has been worthwhile. I still set off with a plan, get distracted by something ridiculous at the side of the road, and lose another hour to a game I thought I'd finished. I laughed within minutes of starting, and I laugh every time I play. I've also been stressed, revolted, astonished, baffled, heartbroken and euphoric. I've run the full gamut of emotions, and I still do each time I return to Vice City.

#8998. Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#8996. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

How it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he says.

What it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

#8995. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Last medically reviewed on June 27, 2024

#8994. Logitech MX Keypad review: Can nine LCD keys take the pain out of Photoshop?

A smart, compact control surface with real potential, the Logitech MX Keypad has plenty of presets and context-aware functions for the best software and utilities, but you’ll only get your money’s worth if you put in the setup time.

Options+ is context-aware and offers presets for popular apps

LCD keys show a changing icon for each function

15 'pages' of custom keys is a ludicrous amount

A good alternative to native drawing tablet remotes

Unsupported apps such as Rebelle and ArtRage need manual setup

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Connection: Wired USB-C, 1.5m USB-C to USB-C

Features: Logi Options+, app-specific, automatically switching

Supported apps: Adobe Creative Cloud, Figma, Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, VS Code, IntelliJ, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Zoom, Slack, Google (beta), and more

I’m always drawn to gadgets that promise to save time or make things easier and more accessible, whether it's the best drawing tablets, shortcut keyboards, or odd little controllers parked next to my mouse: if it claims to shave seconds off a repetitive job, I want to try it. Photoshop is my worst offender, because half the battle is remembering where Adobe has hidden things this time with each new update.

The Logitech MX Keypad is a desktop control pad with nine customisable LCD keys, each showing an icon for whatever you’ve assigned to it. Two physical buttons flip between pages, so you get more shortcuts without another huge peripheral crowding your desk. It's in the Logitech MX line, gadgets aimed as much at creatives as at everyday folk looking to make life easier.

At $99.99 / £89.99, it’s not an impulse buy but something you should consider, and after years of drilling Ctrl, Alt and Shift combos into my left hand, I wasn’t sure I needed one. I also use a drawing tablet and stylus for art, so I have just enough buttons on the pen, or I can access more on my tablet's virtual keyboard. But knowing a shortcut and having a button for the thing you hit countless times an hour, whether it's in Photoshop, calling up Google files or browser pages, is a different matter. That's where the MX keypad aims to be a decent all-rounder for everyday work and creative projects alike.

Nine square keys sit in a three-by-three grid, and because each has its own screen, the icons change based on what you’ve assigned. That beats a traditional macro pad with fixed labels: you can see what a button does instead of memorising obscure combos.

It works with the best digital art software and creative apps, including Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom, Premiere Pro, and Figma. Importantly, it’s context-aware, so you can select your app in Logitech Options+ and it loads presets for that software’s most common tools; from there, you can edit or set up your own actions.

Nine keys run out fast, so using up to 15 'pages' of nine preset buttons (135 total assigned actions) earns it keep as a feature. Overkill, yes, but some will want all that power at a button press. The Options+ app lets you build separate layouts for different jobs, one for Photoshop, another for Lightroom and so on. Rather than living with Adobe’s shortcuts, you build the layout around how you work, and it's as easy as going into the Options+ app and assigning keyboard shortcuts to the buttons, including combinations of buttons, and it supports different saved shortcut collections, so you can also tailor favourites to different apps.

At roughly 92 x 78 x 25mm, it sits beside a mouse and keyboard without taking over, and it's easy to hold, which matters if your desk already hosts a pen tablet or display. A kickstand and a 1.5m USB-C cable come in the box.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

It’s not perfect. The keys lack the click of good mechanical keys, but they do have an old-fashioned soft-push feel, much like an old 90s dial-up digital phone, but that also means you need a little force to push one, and the stand lacks weight or 'stick', so it drifts as you press. The solution? Hold it by the top and depress with my thumb. I do like how each button has its own little digital decal icon showing its function, and you can buy sticky pads to keep it in place.

It’s also wired only, which is a little surprising at this price, but it's not the end of the world, and the cable is long enough for most setups.

For me, the MX Keypad makes the most sense with Photoshop (I've also downloaded and set it up for Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, Google, and Slack), and even fast keyboard users end up wishing something were easier to reach. Favourite brushes, colour swapping and new layers all suit the MX Keypad, and you can split them across pages for selections, masking, painting, and layer management. I’m a light Photoshop user, but I found that adding shortcuts for Lasso selections, favourite brushes, and layer options sped up how I use the software.

When I’m drawing, I don’t want to look down at the keyboard or lift my hand off the tablet, so a few key actions right beside my drawing area help. For the most part, I find the custom buttons on a stylus work well alongside touch controls on a tablet, but if you are more professionally minded and need all the options all the time, a shortcut keypad is essential. While XPPen, Huion, and Xencelabs all offer good remotes, the MX Keypad is a step above, with more buttons, more configuration options, and easy-to-understand icons and button labels.

If you’re already quick on a keyboard, reaching across to press a button may not be any faster. The gain is in the visual reminders and having rarely used commands grouped on pages somewhere easy to find. With only nine keys, you’ll need to plan your pages carefully, but for serious users, once organised, you'll be able to cycle to function collections at speed.

Of course, not all apps are supported; for example, Rebelle and ArtRage aren’t here, but you can add the apps manually and set up profiles and shortcuts based on keyboard commands; it just takes more time than Logitech’s preset app library. Using presets is as simple as clicking a drop-down menu, but adding and editing a new app setup and customising each key can take around 30 minutes per 'page'.

Because profiles are set per app, the buttons change colour and icon designs as you switch software. I found this to be the MX Keypad's strength, because it becomes one device that can follow you around your creative workflow, so if you’re someone who works between software, from Blender to Photoshop, for example, the MX Keypad can follow along.

Options+, the same app used by the MX Master 4 Special Edition mouse, can configure everything, but it takes some time to get used to if you’re editing a new app that isn’t supported out of the box. If you use the most popular, most common software, it’s easy; if you use niche apps, it can feel far from plug-and-play, since you have to manually enter each keyboard command.

For artists and designers who bounce between the biggest and most common apps, it’s a compact way to build your own control pad, and LCD keys beat cryptic labels on a standard macro pad or half-remembered keyboard shortcuts.

At $99.99 / £89.99, the Logitech MX Keypad is a fair price for a quick key remote. By comparison, the Xencelabs Quick Keys cost a similar $99.99 / £95.90 and also have LCD icons, but only words and no images, while the decent XPPen Remote is $49.99 / £49.99 but more basic than both Xencelabs and the Logitech. Both are wireless remotes, unlike the MX Keypad, but as a shortcut remote, the MX Keypad is the best of the three because Options+ offers an easy setup with established software and a huge number of buttons and pages.

But the MX Keypad has more going for it than those remotes: more custom buttons, more context-aware presets, and the option to use ‘pages’, which packs a staggering number of functions onto one face. The big advantage over a traditional drawing tablet remote is two-fold: you get little icons that explain each function, plus the depth of Options+ with multiple pre-loaded shortcuts for the best graphic design software and art apps out of the box.

Do beginners and hobbyists like me need this much choice? I mostly use two to three apps, for example, and three or four functions, and I don't need speed, but if you're a pro with a library of art, design, 3D, and video editing software to pair with and move across in one project, it would be a good gadget. For pros and tinkerers, it’s essential; for everyone else, it may be overkill.
